title: Release build signed with the public Android debug keystore
description:
The release build type is configured to sign with the shared Android debug keystore instead of a private release key. Because the debug keystore and its password are public and identical on every development machine, the shipped release APK is signed with a key any third party can reproduce. Anyone holding that key can build an APK that Android accepts as a legitimate update to this application, and the application can never be published to Google Play under a trustworthy signing identity.

This finding is based on static source review only and is **unconfirmed, not dynamically validated** — no APK was built and no update was delivered in this assessment.
impact: The application's release artifacts are signed with a key that is not secret. If the APK is distributed outside Google Play (which the permission set and feature set make likely for this product), an attacker can produce a tampered APK that carries the same signing identity and installs as an in-place update over the legitimate app, with no signature-mismatch warning to the user. Such an update runs with the application's identity and privileges and can read the app's private data — including the locally stored chat transcripts, the agent memory vault, and the Action Center store — and can exercise every device capability the app has been granted (notifications, accessibility, location, camera, Health Connect). The app also cannot be published to Google Play with this signing configuration, so the release pipeline is not production-ready.
poc_description:
1. Read `android/app/build.gradle.kts` and observe that the `release` build type sets `signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")` and that no `signingConfigs { create("release") { ... } }` block exists.
2. Observe that no `key.properties`, `.jks` or `.keystore` file exists anywhere in the repository, so no private release key is configured.
3. Confirm the shared debug keystore is the only signing material in play by inspecting the Android SDK keystore location and the absence of any release signing properties file.
4. (Not performed — no Android SDK or emulator in this environment) Build a release APK and inspect its signing certificate; it will match the well-known debug certificate fingerprint shared by all Android debug builds.

```bash

sed -n '35,41p' android/app/build.gradle.kts

# 2. Confirm no release signing material exists in the repository
find . -name 'key.properties' -o -name '*.jks' -o -name '*.keystore' | grep -v build/

# 3. Confirm no signingConfigs block was ever defined
grep -n 'signingConfigs' android/app/build.gradle.kts
```
remediation_steps:
1. Generate a private release keystore and store it outside the repository, with the credentials in a `key.properties` file that is already covered by the Android `.gitignore`.
2. Declare a `signingConfigs { create("release") { ... } }` block in `android/app/build.gradle.kts` that loads `key.properties`, and point the `release` build type at that config instead of `debug`.
3. Make the release build fail loudly when `key.properties` is absent, so a debug-signed release can never be produced by accident again.
4. Enable code shrinking and resource shrinking for the release build type (`isMinifyEnabled = true`, `isShrinkResources = true`) and add a ProGuard/R8 keep rules file.
5. Store the release keystore and its passwords in the CI secret store, and use Play App Signing if the app is distributed through Google Play.
6. Rotate the signing identity before any public release — an already-distributed debug-signed build cannot be safely upgraded in place.
evidence:
`android/app/build.gradle.kts` lines 35-41 (verbatim):

```kotlin title=android/app/build.gradle.kts startLineNumber=35 endLineNumber=41

        release {
            // TODO: Add your own signing config for the release build.
            // Signing with the debug keys for now, so `flutter run --release` works.
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")
        }
    }
```

Absence of any release signing material:

```text
$ find . -name 'key.properties' -o -name '*.jks' -o -name '*.keystore' | grep -v build/
(no output)

$ grep -n 'signingConfigs' android/app/build.gradle.kts
39:            signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")
```

The Android `.gitignore` already anticipates a real release keystore, confirming one was intended:

```text
key.properties
**/*.keystore
**/*.jks
```

No `isMinifyEnabled` or `isShrinkResources` property appears anywhere in `android/app/build.gradle.kts`.
assumptions: Assumes the release APK produced from this repository is distributed to users (via sideload, an MDM/enterprise channel, or a third-party store) rather than only being built locally for development. Google Play would reject an APK signed with the debug key, so the Play-distribution scenario is not affected. The update-hijack scenario additionally assumes the victim installs an attacker-supplied APK that presents itself as an update.
counterevidence: Actively checked for constraints that would neutralise this finding. (1) A release `signingConfigs` block or a `key.properties` file could have existed and overridden the debug config — neither is present anywhere in the repository, and `key.properties` is only referenced in `.gitignore`. (2) Gradle could have injected a signing config through a property or an included build — `android/build.gradle.kts` only sets repositories, build directories and JVM targets, and `gradle.properties` contains no signing properties. (3) The impact could be limited to "cannot publish to Play", which would make it informational — but the update-hijack consequence is real for any non-Play distribution channel, which is the realistic channel for this app given its permission set. The genuine constraint that lowers severity is that exploitation requires the attacker to already be able to deliver an APK to the victim and the victim to accept the install, so this is not a remotely triggerable issue on its own; that precondition is reflected in the `attack_complexity` and `user_interaction` metrics rather than being used to dismiss the finding. No dynamic validation was possible, so the exploitability of the update path is reasoned from Android's documented signing behaviour rather than demonstrated.
confidence_rationale: The code fact is certain and directly observable — the release build type is configured with `signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")` and no release signing material exists in the repository. What is not dynamically validated is the downstream consequence: no APK was built, no signing certificate was inspected, and no update-over-install was attempted, because this assessment had no Android SDK, emulator or device. The conclusion that a same-certificate APK installs as an update relies on documented Android platform behaviour rather than on an executed proof.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that release APKs built from this repository are actually distributed to users outside Google Play would raise the severity, because the forgeable update channel would then be live rather than hypothetical; conversely, evidence that the project only ever builds debug artifacts locally (and that the release configuration is unused scaffolding) would reduce this to an informational build-hygiene observation.

## Summary

Stop signing release builds with the shared Android debug keystore.

## Rationale

`android/app/build.gradle.kts` currently points the `release` build type at the built-in `debug` signing config:

```kotlin
    buildTypes {
        release {
            // TODO: Add your own signing config for the release build.
            // Signing with the debug keys for now, so `flutter run --release` works.
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("debug")
        }
    }
```

The debug keystore is generated identically on every Android development machine and its password is public. A release APK signed with it carries a signing identity that any third party can reproduce, so a tampered APK can be accepted by Android as an in-place update to this application. The app also cannot be published to Google Play with this configuration.

The repository already anticipates a real release keystore — `android/.gitignore` lists `key.properties`, `**/*.keystore` and `**/*.jks` — but the Gradle wiring was never completed and no keystore is present.

## Changes

- Add a `signingConfigs { create("release") { ... } }` block that loads credentials from `key.properties`.
- Fail the build with a clear message when `key.properties` is missing, so a debug-signed release can never be produced accidentally.
- Point the `release` build type at the new config.
- Enable `isMinifyEnabled` and `isShrinkResources` for release, which were previously unset.

## Follow-up for the maintainer

Create a private release keystore, place it outside the repository, and add a matching `key.properties`:

```properties
storePassword=<password>
keyPassword=<password>
keyAlias=<alias>
storeFile=<absolute path to the .jks>
```

Store the same values in the CI secret store, and rotate the signing identity before any public release — an already-distributed debug-signed build cannot be upgraded in place safely.

title: Sensitive app data included in Android backups because allowBackup is unset
description: The application declares no android:allowBackup attribute on its application element and ships no fullBackupContent or dataExtractionRules rule, so Android applies its default of allowBackup=true and includes the app private data in cloud backups and device-to-device transfers. The app keeps sensitive user content in plaintext app-private stores - chat transcripts, the agent memory vault, imported skills and the Action Center inbox - which are consequently swept into the backup set without any exclusion. This finding is based on static source review only and is unconfirmed, not dynamically validated: no device, emulator or backup extraction was available in this assessment.
impact: The app private storage is included in Android cloud backups and device-to-device transfers. A backup set obtained through ADB backup, a cloud-account compromise, or forensic acquisition of a backup image yields the plaintext contents of flames_memory.db (the agent memory vault, whose content column holds arbitrary user- and agent-authored text), flames_skills.db, and the Hive action_center box, together with the session titles in flames_chat.db. The LLM API key and server-profile records are held in FlutterSecureStorage and are not directly recoverable from a backup because Android excludes the Keystore master key, and chat message bodies are likewise encrypted at rest rather than stored in flames_chat.db; the exposure is therefore user content rather than credentials or full transcripts. The issue also runs the other way: a backup restored onto a different device reintroduces this data into app storage without the user having chosen to restore it.
technical_analysis:
Android includes an application's private data in cloud backup and device-to-device transfer when android:allowBackup is true, which is the platform default when the attribute is omitted. The application element in android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml declares no allowBackup, fullBackupContent or dataExtractionRules attribute, and no such resource file exists under android/app/src/main/res/xml/ (that directory contains only accessibility_service_config.xml). The default therefore applies and the whole app data directory is backed up.

The data directory contains plaintext stores traced in code:

- flames_chat.db in the app databases directory (chat_local_datasource.dart:26,64). Its schema (chat_local_datasource.dart:80-95) contains a single `sessions` table: id, profile_id, title, created_at, updated_at. Message bodies are deliberately not stored here — `saveMessages` writes them through FlutterSecureStorage (`_storage.write(key: keyFor(sessionId), value: encoded)`, chat_local_datasource.dart:113-125) and `getMessages` reads them back from the same store (:240-261). The plaintext exposure from this database is therefore the session titles, which are derived verbatim from the first 40 characters of the user's first message (chat_repository_impl.dart:22-28, agent_cubit.dart:162-168), not the transcripts themselves.
- flames_memory.db in the app databases directory on Android (sqlite_memory_datasource.dart:16,88-103), holding the memories table and its FTS5 mirror. This store is plaintext and its `content` column holds arbitrary user- and agent-authored text.
- flames_skills.db in the app databases directory (skills_local_datasource.dart:15).
- the Hive action_center box opened under the app documents directory by Hive.initFlutter('flames') (lib/myapp.dart:47), storing JSON-encoded inbox entries with free-text titles, summaries and action payloads (lib/data/models/action_center/action_item_model.dart:39-55).

None is excluded by a backup rule, so all are included in the backup set. Android 12+ would honour a dataExtractionRules resource, but the attribute is unset, so no restriction is in force on any supported API level. Credentials (LLM API key, server profiles) are held in FlutterSecureStorage and are not recoverable from a backup because Android excludes the Keystore master key.

```sql title=lib/data/datasources/local/memory/sqlite_memory_datasource.dart startLineNumber=130 endLineNumber=137
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
        key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,

        tags TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',

        updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL

```

Credentials are held separately in FlutterSecureStorage (lib/data/datasources/local/settings/secure_storage_service.dart:41-42, instantiated with default options at lib/common/injection/modules.dart:23), so they are not directly exposed by this issue - but that protection does not extend to the plaintext stores above.

counterevidence: Looked for constraints that would neutralise this. No fullBackupContent or dataExtractionRules attribute or resource exists anywhere under android/, so nothing is excluded. The stores are not outside the auto-backup set: flames_chat.db and flames_skills.db resolve to the app databases directory, flames_memory.db resolves there on Android, and the Hive action_center box resolves under the app documents directory. The genuine constraint is that the credentials themselves live in FlutterSecureStorage with default options, and Android excludes the Keystore master key from backup, so the stored LLM API key and base URL are not directly recoverable from a backup set. That is why confidentiality is rated Low rather than High. It reduces the value of the extracted data but does not neutralise the finding, because the chat transcripts, memory-vault rows and Action Center entries are plaintext SQLite and Hive files with no such protection. No dynamic validation was possible.
confidence_rationale: The static evidence is complete: no allowBackup, dataExtractionRules or fullBackupContent attribute exists anywhere in the Android configuration, and the sensitive stores were traced in code to app-private paths. What is not validated is the end-to-end extraction: no device, emulator, ADB or bmgr access was available, so no backup set was produced or parsed. The step from an unset attribute to data leaving the device is documented Android behaviour, not an executed proof.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrating that a produced backup set contains readable chat-transcript or memory-vault rows would raise the severity; evidence that the app is only distributed to managed devices with cloud backup disabled by policy would lower it.

## Summary

Exclude the app private data from Android cloud backup and device-to-device transfer.

## Rationale

The application element declares no android:allowBackup attribute and the project ships no fullBackupContent or dataExtractionRules rule, so Android applies its default of allowBackup=true. The app stores sensitive user content in plaintext app-private files:

- flames_chat.db - chat transcripts
- flames_memory.db - the agent memory vault
- flames_skills.db - imported skill definitions
- the Hive action_center box opened under Hive.initFlutter('flames')

All of these sit inside the auto-backup include set and are swept into cloud backups and device transfers.

## Changes

- Set android:allowBackup="false" on the application element.
- Add android:dataExtractionRules="@xml/data_extraction_rules" pointing at a new resource that excludes the root, database, sharedpref and file domains from both cloud-backup and device-transfer, so the exclusion is explicit and reviewable on Android 12+.

## Follow-up for the maintainer

If chat history should later survive a device migration, replace the blanket exclusion with a targeted rule that includes only non-sensitive stores and explicitly excludes the three databases and the Hive box directory - or implement a user-initiated, encrypted export instead of relying on the platform backup channel.

title: Exported MainActivity accepts unvalidated action extra, letting any co-resident Android app start a microphone voice turn and dispatch agent prompts
description: The exported `MainActivity` of the Flames Android app reads the string extra `extra_flames_action` from any incoming `Intent` and forwards it, unvalidated, to the Flutter layer, which dispatches on it without an allowlist. Any third-party app installed on the same device can therefore start `MainActivity` with a crafted extra and trigger privileged app behaviour with no user action beyond the app window becoming visible: `voice_input` starts a 15-second speech-recognition (microphone) capture session, and `quick_status` sends a canned prompt to the AI agent, which may then execute device tools. **This finding is unconfirmed and not dynamically validated — the audit was source-only with no emulator or device.**
impact:
An attacker with no Android permissions and no special access — merely a co-resident app on the same device — can drive Flames' most sensitive local capability without the user tapping anything in the app.

1. **Microphone activation (`voice_input`).** The app opens a 15-second speech-recognition session (`VoiceTurnService.defaultListenFor`). Any speech in the room during that window is transcribed on-device and, when a dispatch transport is ready, transmitted to the configured remote LLM API as a chat prompt. The capture begins with the microphone permission already granted by the user to Flames, so no permission dialog appears. The recording indicator is an overlay bubble that only exists if the user previously enabled it (off by default), so in the default configuration there is no on-screen indication that capture is active.

2. **Autonomous agent dispatch (`quick_status`).** The fixed prompt `Quick status check: summarize battery, device context, and agent readiness.` is injected into the agent loop. The agent can respond by invoking the app's native device tools (clipboard, location, contacts, calendar, notifications, accessibility-tree reading, Health Connect). The dispatch path was read to confirm the resulting state machine, and a `WaitingApproval` terminal state is surfaced as a failure rather than silently bypassing the human-in-the-loop gate, so this leg is bounded by the existing tier gating rather than escalating it.

3. **Persistence and reachability.** `pendingAction` is set on both `onCreate` and `onNewIntent` and is never cleared until the Dart layer drains it, so the value survives a cold start and is replayed when the listener mounts. The chain does not require the app to be in the foreground: the action is delivered through `onNewIntent` while the activity is already alive, and the background service path (`FlamesBackgroundService` action `ACTION_VOICE_INPUT`, reachable from the ongoing notification and the Quick Settings tile) performs the same Dart injection. Injected microphone capture is the demonstrated consequence; no audio exfiltration to an attacker-controlled destination is demonstrated, so the confidentiality rating below reflects initiation of capture of the user's audio, not demonstrated attacker retrieval of it.
technical_analysis:
## Root cause

`MainActivity` is declared exported with no guarding permission, which is required for the launcher entry point:

```xml title=android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml startLineNumber=57 endLineNumber=76
<activity
    android:name=".MainActivity"
    android:exported="true"
    android:launchMode="singleTop"
    ...
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN"/>
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER"/>
    </intent-filter>
```

`extractActionFromIntent()` accepts an arbitrary string from that `Intent` and stores it, with no allowlist, no caller-identity check and no signature/authentication of the caller:

```kotlin title=android/app/src/main/kotlin/ai/hermes/flames/MainActivity.kt startLineNumber=73 endLineNumber=85
private fun extractActionFromIntent(intent: Intent?): String? {
    val actionExtra = intent?.getStringExtra("extra_flames_action")
    if (!actionExtra.isNullOrBlank()) {
        pendingAction = actionExtra
        return actionExtra
    }
    if (intent?.action == FlamesQuickTile.ACTION_QUICK_TILE_TRIGGER) {
        val fallbackAction = "voice_input"
        pendingAction = fallbackAction
        return fallbackAction
    }
    return null
}
```

The value is delivered to Dart on both lifecycle paths — cold start (`onCreate`, line 56) and warm delivery (`onNewIntent`, lines 59-66) — and is additionally readable by the Flutter layer through the `getPendingAction` / `clearPendingAction` methods on the `ai.hermes.flames/background_service` channel (lines 303-309). `FlamesBackgroundService.EXTRA_ACTION` (line 38) is the same string constant, and the ongoing notification's "Quick Status" action ships the same extra (lines 402-406), confirming the extra is a first-class control channel rather than a developer leftover.

## Sink chain

1. `VoiceTurnActionListener._handleAction` switches on the action value with no validation:
```dart title=lib/presentation/voice/voice_turn_action_listener.dart startLineNumber=162 endLineNumber=178
void _handleAction(String action) {
  switch (action.toLowerCase().trim()) {
    case 'voice_input':
      unawaited(_runTurnWithTileSync());
      break;
    case 'cancel_voice':
      unawaited(_cancelTurnAndResetTile());
      break;
    case 'quick_status':
      unawaited(
        _registry?.active?.dispatch(
```

Treat the action extra as untrusted input at the Android boundary, because any co-resident app can supply it.

fix_pr_body:
## Summary

Validate the `extra_flames_action` intent extra against an explicit allowlist before it can reach the Flutter layer, closing an unauthorised action-injection path through the exported `MainActivity`.

## Problem

`MainActivity` must be exported to serve as the launcher entry point, but it also acts as a privileged control surface: `extractActionFromIntent()` reads the `extra_flames_action` string from any incoming `Intent` and forwards it, unvalidated, to Dart, where `VoiceTurnActionListener._handleAction` dispatches on it with no allowlist. Any co-resident app can therefore start the activity with `extra_flames_action=voice_input` and open a 15-second speech-recognition (microphone) session, or send `quick_status` to inject a prompt into the agent loop, with no user action inside the app.

No caller-identity check (`getCallingActivity` / `getCallingPackage` / `Binder.getCallingUid`) exists anywhere in the Android sources, and the activity carries no guarding `android:permission`.

## Fix

- Add an `ALLOWED_ACTIONS` set containing exactly the three actions the app implements: `voice_input`, `cancel_voice`, `quick_status`.
- Reject any other value in `extractActionFromIntent()` by returning `null`, so `pendingAction` is never set and nothing is forwarded over the method channel.
- The check lives in the single extraction function, so both the cold-start (`onCreate`) and warm (`onNewIntent`) paths are covered.

## Behaviour preserved

- Launcher start (no extra) is unchanged.
- Quick Settings tile trigger still falls back to `voice_input`.
- All three ongoing-notification actions (`Voice Input`, `Quick Status`, `Stop`) carry values inside the allowlist.
- The read-only contract test `test/domain/tools/chat/quick_tile_contract_test.dart` assertions on `MainActivity.kt` still hold.

## Residual risk (out of scope for this patch)

The allowlist bounds the accepted *values*, not the *caller*: an attacker can still trigger a legitimate `voice_input` turn. Fully restricting third-party automation requires moving it behind a signature-level permission on a dedicated exported component — a product decision tracked in the finding's remediation steps.

## Verification

Static trace of source → sink through the patched code; no compiler, device or test run was available in the audit environment, so the change was reviewed by inspection only.

description: The Android agent can read the accessibility tree of whatever app is in the foreground and hand that text to the LLM as a tool result (`ui_find_elements`). The codebase already ships a prompt-injection scanner (`SkillSecurityScanner`) but applies it only to imported skill text, so screen content reaches the model unframed and unscanned. The same model can then call Tier-1 tools that need no user approval (`save_memory`, `clipboard_write`) and read Tier-1/2 sensitive data (clipboard, location, files, notifications, OTP, health, contacts). Memory entries are re-injected on later turns as a `role: "system"` message, which converts transient screen text into persistent, highest-authority instructions. **Unconfirmed, not dynamically validated** — this is a source-only audit; there is no emulator, no device and no running app, so no payload was executed against a live model.
impact: Attacker-authored text on screen gains instruction authority inside a tool-calling agent. A malicious app that renders a crafted window (or a hostile web page / message rendered in any app) and waits for the user to invoke the agent can attempt to steer the model into data-collecting tool calls, and to persist the payload into the memory vault where it is re-injected as a system message on every subsequent turn. Because the injected text can invoke `save_memory` (Tier 1, auto-executed, no approval) and `clipboard_write` (Tier 1), the payload can be made persistent and can be staged for collection by a co-resident app. Read tools that need no approval include `list_device_files`, `read_web_page`, `calendar_list_events`, `external_camera_list`, `search_memories` and `list_memories`. technical_analysis:
**1. The collected data.** `FlamesAccessibilityService.captureTree()` walks the foreground window and emits `text`, `contentDescription` and `packageName` for every node, with no exclusion of secure fields. The service config enables `canRetrieveWindowContent="true"` and `flagRetrieveInteractiveWindows`, so the tree of any foreground app is readable.

**2. The pull-only path.** Capture is strictly on demand: `captureTree()` is reached only from the `getScreenTree` method-channel handler, which is reached only from the Dart platform wrapper, which is reached only from `findElementsFormatted`. Nothing is pushed to Dart on accessibility events — `onAccessibilityEvent` only records `lastEventPackage`, which is never read. There is no background or continuous collection.

**3. No framing, no scan.** `findElementsFormatted` returns `AccessibilityTreeSerializer.serialize(...)` directly, and that string becomes the tool result content. The only transformation applied is `_sanitize`, which strips newlines/tabs and replaces double quotes with single quotes — a display-formatting step, not an injection control. The repo's own prompt-injection scanner (`SkillSecurityScanner`, twelve patterns including chatml delimiters and instruction overrides) has exactly one production caller, `SkillImportService.buildPreview`, so it never sees screen text. There is no untrusted-data marker anywhere on this path, and the assembled messages are serialized and posted verbatim to the configured chat-completions endpoint.

**4. Amplifier — persistent system-role injection.** `save_memory` is registered as `SecurityTier.tier1Auto`, so the model can write memory with no user approval. On a later turn, matching memories are inserted into the request as a message with `'role': 'system'`, i.e. the highest-authority position available. Attacker-influenced text therefore survives the conversation it arrived in and is re-presented as an instruction to the model.

**5. Missing redaction (observation, not an independent claim).** `captureTree()` never calls `AccessibilityNodeInfo.isPassword()`; the identifier appears nowhere in the Android or Dart trees. Documented Android behaviour is that an accessibility service holding `canRetrieveWindowContent` can read password-field text, and that redaction is device/OEM dependent — so the client-side absence of an exclusion is the only thing this audit can establish. Whether the platform already redacts on a given device was **not** verified here; the fix therefore skips password nodes client-side rather than relying on the platform.

remediation_steps:
Treat every accessibility-tree result as untrusted data before it becomes a tool result, and stop relying on the platform to redact secure fields.

1. Frame the tool result explicitly at the single point where the tree is turned into text (the data-layer `findElementsFormatted`). Prefix and suffix the serialized tree with a short, unambiguous statement that the block is screen content captured from another app, that it must be treated strictly as data, and that nothing inside it may change the agent's task, tool policy, or disclosures. Leave the empty-tree message unframed so existing behaviour is preserved.
2. Reuse the existing prompt-injection scanner rather than writing a new one. Screen text is the same untrusted class as an imported skill body, so run `SkillSecurityScanner` over the serialized tree and, when patterns match, prepend the matched pattern identifiers so the model and the user can see that the screen contains a suspected payload. Because the scanner is pattern-based and evadable by paraphrase, keep the explicit framing as the primary control and treat the scan as defence in depth.
3. Exclude secure fields on the device side. In `captureTree`, skip nodes whose `isPassword` flag is set, and skip their subtrees, so password and other secure-field values are never collected even if a given device does not redact them.
4. State the data class in the tool description so the model's own tool contract carries the warning, not just the result payload.
5. Apply the same framing to the other untrusted text channels that feed the prompt — notification text, web-page text, and recalled memory entries — and stop injecting recalled memory as a `role: "system"` message, which currently gives attacker-influenced text the highest available authority. fix_pr_body:
## Frame accessibility-tree output as untrusted data

### Problem

`ui_find_elements` reads the accessibility tree of whatever app is in the foreground and hands the serialized text to the model as a tool result. That text is authored by *another app*, not by Flames or the user, but nothing on the path marks it as untrusted and the repo's existing prompt-injection scanner (`SkillSecurityScanner`) is never applied to it — its only production caller is the skill-import service. The model can then call Tier-1 tools that need no approval, including `save_memory`, whose contents are re-injected on later turns as a `role: "system"` message.

### Change

- **Frame the tool result.** `findElementsFormatted` now wraps a non-empty tree in an explicit untrusted-data statement (`AccessibilityMessages.untrustedFraming`) before it can become tool-result content. The empty-tree message is short-circuited and returned unchanged.
- **Reuse the existing scanner.** A small `AccessibilityTreeInjectionScanner` runs `SkillSecurityScanner` over the serialized tree and prepends the matched pattern ids, so a suspected payload is visible to the model and the user. Screen text is never blocked — only framed and annotated — because dropping a legitimate screen would break the tool.
- **Stop collecting secure fields on the device.** `captureTree` skips nodes with `isPassword` set, and their subtrees, rather than relying on device-dependent platform redaction.
- **Say it in the tool contract.** The `ui_find_elements` description now states that the returned text is authored by the foreground app and must be treated as untrusted data.

### Why this shape

The framing is the primary control because it does not depend on pattern matching; the scanner is defence in depth and is evadable by paraphrase, so it is additive rather than load-bearing. The fix is placed at the single production seam where the tree becomes text, so every existing call path is covered without touching the serializer or the registry.

### Follow-up (not in this change)

Notification text, web-page text and recalled memory are the same untrusted class and remain unframed; recalled memory is still injected as a `role: "system"` message, which gives attacker-influenced text the highest available authority. Those should be addressed separately.

### Testing

Exact-string assertions live at the serializer and registry layers and are untouched; the data-layer tests use `contains`, and the empty-tree case is preserved exactly. Analyzer and test runs were not possible in the audit environment (no Dart/Flutter/Android SDK available) — please run `flutter analyze` and the accessibility test suites before merging.

title: Tools with device-state side effects are classified Tier 1 "Read-Only / Ambient" and auto-execute with no authorization gate
description: The agent tool registry documents Tier 1 as **"Read-Only / Ambient (auto-execute)"**, but six registered tools that modify device state, send user-visible output, or destroy user data are assigned to Tier 1 and therefore execute with no permission check and no approval prompt. Two of them (`send_local_notification`, `save_memory`) additionally give an injected instruction a user-visible spoofing primitive and a persistence foothold, because saved memories are re-injected into every subsequent model request as a `role: system` message. The misclassification is provably a defect rather than policy: `send_local_notification` (Tier 1, auto-executes) and `schedule_reminder` (Tier 3, requires a user tap) are registered against the same notification service in the same method, so sending a notification immediately is ungated while scheduling one for later is gated.
impact: Once the on-device agent has decided to call one of these tools, the action executes with no permission evaluation and no user confirmation. The demonstrated (static) consequences are: arbitrary attacker-influenced text written to the system clipboard; arbitrary user-visible local notifications presented under the application's identity (a spoofing primitive that can impersonate a bank, security, or system alert); the ability to start and stop the foreground service, acquire and release wake locks, and set the Quick Settings tile state; registration of persistent geofence monitoring; and destruction of the user's stored memory vault by id or key with no confirmation. Because `save_memory` writes to a SQLite vault whose contents are re-injected into every subsequent model request as a `role: system` message, an instruction that reaches the prompt can also persist attacker-authored text inside the system-role portion of the conversation, surviving the turn, the session, and application restarts. The affected scope is the local device state and local application data of the user who runs the agent; no disclosure of restricted data was demonstrated.

The strongest case against this finding, argued in full:

**1. Model cooperation is required and is stochastic.** Nothing here forces the model to call a tool. An attacker who lands injected text still depends on a non-deterministic model choosing the affected tool. This genuinely limits the finding and is why attack complexity is rated High rather than Low.

**2. Attacker-controlled text must first reach the prompt.** That requires either the user having granted Flames notification-listener access to a hostile app, or the agent fetching attacker content. This is a real precondition and is reflected in the rating.

Under that reading, `send_local_notification` is Tier 1 because it needs no permission prompt of its own, and `schedule_reminder` is Tier 3 because scheduling is a destructive-style operation. That reading fails for three independent reasons. First, the enum's own documentation states the semantics: Tier 1 is "Read-Only / Ambient", and Tier 3 is "State-Modifying / Destructive" — under the stated contract, a tool that modifies state cannot be Tier 1. Second, under the "no OS permission" reading the classification is still internally inconsistent: sending a notification immediately and scheduling one for later both call the same service and neither requires a distinct runtime permission beyond `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`, yet they are placed in opposite tiers. Third, the tool descriptions written by the authors themselves contradict their own tier assignment — `schedule_reminder` is described as "(requires user confirmation)" while the immediate notification carries no such warning, even though it is the more direct action. The application's own bundled skill metadata also labels the notification tools "Tier 2 Perm", a third answer that matches neither assignment.

fix_pr_body:
## Summary

Several agent tools that modify device state are registered at the automatic tier and therefore execute with no permission evaluation and no user confirmation, contradicting the tier contract documented in the security policy. This change moves them to the confirmation tier and stops presenting stored memory content to the model as trusted system context.

## Problem

The security policy defines the automatic tier as "Read-Only / Ambient", but the following tools are registered there despite having side effects:

| Tool | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `send_local_notification` | Sends a user-visible notification with model-controlled title and body |
| `clipboard_write` | Writes arbitrary text to the system clipboard |
| `save_memory` | Persists an entry in the local memory vault |
| `delete_memory` | Deletes stored memories by id or key |
| `register_geofence` | Registers persistent location monitoring |
| `manage_background_service` | Starts/stops the foreground service, manages wake locks and the Quick Settings tile |

The single gate in the agent loop only pauses for the confirmation tier, and the registry gate evaluates permissions only for the permission tier, so none of these tools is checked before execution.

The classification is inconsistent on its own terms: `send_local_notification` and `schedule_reminder` are registered against the same notification service in the same method, yet the immediate notification is automatic while the scheduled reminder requires a user tap.

`save_memory` compounds the issue. Saved entries are re-injected into every model request as a system-role message without an untrusted-data delimiter, so an instruction that reaches the prompt can persist attacker-authored text in the system-role portion of the conversation across turns, sessions, and restarts.

## Changes

1. Move the six tools listed above from the automatic tier to the confirmation tier. The confirmation tier is used rather than the permission tier because none of the underlying services defines a permission callback, and the registry only evaluates permissions when a callback is present — the permission tier would be a silent no-op for these tools.
2. Update the tier documentation so that the automatic tier is explicitly reserved for tools with no device-visible or persistent side effect.
3. Wrap the injected memory block in an untrusted-data directive and encode the stored keys and content so embedded line breaks cannot impersonate the surrounding conversation structure.

## Impact on behavior

The affected tools now require a single confirmation before executing. The legitimate flows continue to work; the memory write path gains one confirmation per write, which is the intended cost for a persistent state change. If an automatic memory-write path is desired, add a permission callback to the memory service and use the permission tier instead.

## Tests

Existing tests that assert the previous tiers, and the integration tests that exercise these tools through the agent loop without an approval step, need to be updated to expect the approval gate. A regression test asserting that no tool performing a write, a notification, a clipboard operation, or an external launch is registered at the automatic tier would prevent this from recurring.

title: Tier-2 permission gate fails open for tools registered without a permission checker
description: The agent tool registry enforces its "Tier 2 — permissioned" security tier with a condition that also tests whether the tool declares a permission checker. A tool registered as Tier 2 without that checker therefore skips permission evaluation entirely and auto-executes exactly like a Tier 1 tool. Seven registrations are in this state, five of them silently (no explanatory comment and no equivalent check inside the underlying service). Because the ReAct loop and the remote gateway RPC path both treat every non-Tier-3 tool as auto-executable, model output and server-supplied tool calls can invoke these device capabilities with no in-application permission evaluation. Unconfirmed, not dynamically validated: no emulator, device, or Flutter toolchain was available, so no tool call was executed.
impact: The application's declared authorization invariant — that a Tier 2 capability runs only after its runtime permission is evaluated — is not enforced for tools registered without a checker. The two most consequential affected tools are `launch_system_setting`, which can navigate the user to the notification-listener, accessibility, and overlay-apps settings pages (the exact pages that grant this app additional device authority), and `open_email_composer`, which can prefill an outbound message. Both can be driven by untrusted text reaching the model, with no in-app confirmation. The demonstrated effect is bounded: the operating system toggle and the mail client's send button still require a user action, so no permission is granted and no message is sent by the tool call itself. The remaining affected tools are neutralised by other controls (scheme allow-list, OS capture UI, physical NFC tap). The durable risk is that the gate silently degrades any future Tier 2 tool that omits the field.

`SecurityTier` documents the intended contract as *"Tier 2: Sensitive / Permissioned (auto-execute only if runtime permission is granted)"* (`lib/domain/tools/chat/security_policy.dart:1-10`), and `SecurityPolicy.requiresPermission` returns true for that tier (`security_policy.dart:26-28`). The registry is the single place that contract is enforced:

```dart title=lib/domain/tools/chat/tool_registry.dart startLineNumber=250 endLineNumber=256

          tool.checkPermission != null) {
        final granted = await tool.checkPermission!();
```

fix_pr_body:
## Make the Tier-2 permission gate fail closed

### Problem

`ToolRegistry.executeTool` enforces the Tier 2 ("permissioned") security tier with a condition that also tests whether the tool declares a permission checker:

```dart
if (SecurityPolicy.requiresPermission(tool.securityTier) &&
    tool.checkPermission != null) {
```

When a tool is registered as `SecurityTier.tier2Permission` but omits `checkPermission`, the second conjunct is false, the whole block is skipped, and the tool executes exactly like a Tier 1 tool. Seven registrations are currently in this state. Because both the ReAct loop and the remote gateway RPC path treat every non-Tier-3 tool as auto-executable, and because the tool name and arguments come from model output or a server-supplied frame, these capabilities can be invoked with no in-application permission evaluation.

### Change

- **Fail closed at the gate.** A Tier 2 tool that declares no checker is refused before its `execute` closure runs.
- **Make deliberate omissions explicit.** Add a `selfEnforcesPermission` marker to `RegisteredTool`, defaulting to `false`. The gate cannot otherwise distinguish a forgotten checker from an intended one, and the accessibility tool relies on service-side evaluation to return a status-specific error.
- **Mark the two genuinely self-enforcing registrations**: `ui_find_elements` (the service refuses to read the tree unless the service is active, via `checkStatus()`) and `camera_take_photo` (the OS capture Activity performs the runtime request itself, so a check-only probe would block first-use capture).

### Follow-up required in the same release

Five registrations have no runtime permission to evaluate and will now fail closed: `open_external_url`, `open_email_composer`, `launch_system_setting`, `nfc_read_tag`, and `nfc_read_emoney_balance`. Each needs its tier resolved — `launch_system_setting` and `open_email_composer` should require human approval, since they land the user on privilege-granting settings pages or create an outbound message the user did not author; the NFC tools and the URL launcher are non-permissioned, since NFC has no runtime permission and requires a physical tap, and the launcher already restricts schemes to http and https. The existing execution tests for these tools will need updating alongside the tier decision.

### Testing

A registry-level invariant test should assert that every registered tool whose tier is not Tier 1 declares either a permission checker or the self-enforcement marker, so a future omission fails the build rather than silently bypassing the gate.

title: Unrestricted file read and unbounded directory enumeration via read_device_file / list_device_files agent tools
description:
The agent tools **`read_device_file`** and **`list_device_files`** accept an absolute filesystem path supplied by the language model and pass it to `File(path).readAsBytes()` / `Directory(path).list()` without any containment check against a workspace root. The declared "device workspace" boundary exists only in the tools' prose descriptions and is never enforced in code.

The one gate that was supposed to constrain `read_device_file` is inert: its Tier-2 permission check resolves to a hardcoded `true`. **`list_device_files` is declared Tier-1 (auto-execute) and therefore has no gate at all**, and it accepts `recursive: true`.

Both paths are reachable from remote model output — tool-call arguments are decoded from the model's JSON with no validation and auto-executed. Because untrusted text (notification bodies, remote skill packages, tool results) reaches the model with no data/instruction separation, a prompt-injection payload can direct the agent to read or enumerate files. **Unconfirmed, not dynamically validated** — this is a source-only audit with no emulator, no device and no running app.
impact:
An attacker who influences the model's tool-call arguments (a remote or compromised model endpoint, a remote skill package, a crafted notification body, or an indirect injection via any tool result) can direct the agent to read and enumerate files as the application's own UID, with no workspace boundary enforced.

**Demonstrated by code path (not runtime-verified):**

- **Unbounded directory enumeration — fully effective.** `list_device_files` is Tier 1 (auto-execute, no gate) and accepts `recursive: true`. It returns names, absolute paths, sizes, modification times and extensions for the whole subtree. Directory listing applies no content filter of any kind, so it enumerates the app's entire private storage — including the `databases/`, `shared_prefs/`, `files/` and `app_flutter/` trees. This discloses the storage layout and reveals which features hold data, which is meaningful reconnaissance for follow-on attacks and is not blocked by any control.
- **Read of NUL-free text files within the app's UID.** `read_device_file` returns any text file the app can open, including application-private XML and JSON. This includes the FlutterSecureStorage backing file under the app's `shared_prefs/` directory (the app constructs `const FlutterSecureStorage()` with no options override at `lib/common/injection/modules.dart:22-23`, so plugin defaults determine the filename; the exact name was not observed on a device). That file holds the **encrypted** credential blobs for the API key, gateway token and server profiles. Because these are ciphertext, this does not by itself disclose the credentials — it discloses the encrypted material, the stored key names, and the existence and structure of the credential store.
- **Filter bypass via the PDF branch.** A path ending in `.pdf` is routed to PDF text extraction *before* the extension denylist and null-byte checks run, and `extractPdfText` applies neither filter. Any file addressed under a `.pdf` name is therefore read with no binary screening at all.

**Explicitly NOT demonstrated, contrary to an earlier draft of this finding:** the plaintext SQLite databases (`flames_memory.db`, `flames_skills.db`, `flames_chat.db`) are **not** readable through `read_device_file`. They are blocked twice over — `db`/`sqlite` appear in the extension denylist, and a real SQLite file contains a NUL byte at offset 15 of its header, which the null-byte sample rejects regardless of filename. Memory-vault contents are also already available to the model through the Tier-1 `list_memories` / `search_memories` tools, so reading the database file would add little.

**Why this is still a finding.** The app intends a workspace boundary — its own bundled skill descriptor states the invariant "read file contents within allowed directories" — and no code enforces it. The absence of containment is the root defect: any future text file the app writes into its private storage (a token cache, a log, an export) becomes immediately readable by model output, and enumeration of the private tree is ungated today. Scope limits, stated honestly: no `READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` / `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` is declared, so arbitrary `/sdcard` reads fail on modern Android; impact is confined to the app's own private storage.

## Summary

`read_device_file` and `list_device_files` pass a model-supplied absolute path straight to `File(path).readAsBytes()` / `Directory(path).list()` with no containment check. The "device workspace" boundary exists only in the tool descriptions. This change makes that boundary real.

## Root cause

- `read_device_file` declares `SecurityTier.tier2Permission`, but its `checkPermission` resolves to `DefaultFileSystemWrapper.checkPermission()`, which is hardcoded `async => true` (`file_workspace_service.dart:78`). The registry's only gate (`tool_registry.dart:250-255`) therefore always passes.
- `list_device_files` is declared `SecurityTier.tier1Auto` and has no gate at all, yet accepts an arbitrary `directoryPath` and `recursive`.
- `readFile` (`file_workspace_service.dart:149-175`) applies only a binary-extension denylist and a null-byte sample. There is no canonicalisation, no base-directory join and no symlink resolution. `getDocumentsDirectory()` is used solely for PDF writes.

## Changes

1. Add `isWithinWorkspace(String path)` to `FileWorkspaceServiceBase` as the single containment primitive.
2. Implement it by resolving the requested path against the application documents directory, lexically collapsing dot segments and normalising separators, then re-checking containment after `resolveSymbolicLinks()` on both the candidate and the root, so a symlink planted inside the workspace cannot escape it.
3. Enforce it in the `execute` closure of both tools, the single point where the model-supplied argument enters, returning `ValidationFailure` when the path is outside the workspace.
4. Replace the hardcoded `true` permission check with a real evaluation of whether the workspace root is resolvable.
5. Raise `list_device_files` from Tier 1 to Tier 2 so it is no longer auto-executed, and bound the directory listing in `listFiles` as defence in depth.

## Verification

- Containment logic executed in isolation against a real filesystem: 16/16 cases correct, including traversal, sibling-prefix confusion and a symlink escape that a lexical-only check would have allowed.
- All three patched files parse cleanly (`dart format --output=none`).
- Legitimate behaviour preserved: in-workspace paths, the workspace root itself, and `dir/..` remain accepted; the user-driven file-picker flow (`chat_screen.dart:880`) is unaffected because containment is enforced at the tool boundary, not inside the shared `readFile`.
- No test files needed changing: the only other implementers of the interface are Mockito mocks, which satisfy added members automatically.

## Note for reviewers

A package-wide `dart analyze`/`dart test` could not be run in this environment (no resolved dependencies, no network). Please run the Flutter test suite before merging.

title: Tier-2 OTP extraction tool bypasses the app's own sensitive-notification filter and transmits a live second-factor code off-device without per-use confirmation
description: The Flames agent tool `extract_latest_otp` extracts a live one-time passcode from another application's notification and returns the code to the configured large-language-model endpoint, while the application's own privacy filter deliberately excludes those same OTP and banking notifications from its sibling notification-reading tool. The tool is classified Tier 2 "permissioned", which means it executes automatically once Notification Listener access has been granted a single time, with no per-use user confirmation — so the one control the application built to keep second-factor codes away from the model is bypassed by a path that then transmits the code off the device.
impact: A live second-factor code — together with the sending application's name, package identifier, and a body snippet — is extracted from another application's notification and transmitted off the device to the configured large-language-model endpoint, and on the gateway path to the remote Hermes server, without any per-use user confirmation. Because the extraction path never consults `isSensitive`, the application's own exclusion of OTP, banking, and password notifications from the model is defeated: the one notification class the product deliberately withholds from the model is the exact class this tool hands over. Nothing binds the extracted code to a transaction the user initiated, and no confirmation step exists, so the code is disclosed to a third party that has no functional need for it. The repository's own end-to-end test further has the model persist the extracted code into the long-term memory vault via the auto-executing Tier-1 `save_memory` tool, and that vault is a plain, unencrypted SQLite database (`flames_memory.db`), which extends the window in which the code is readable at rest. On a device that receives OTPs for banking, email, or account recovery, this converts a short-lived authentication secret into a durable third-party disclosure.
technical_analysis:
**The two notification paths disagree.** `NotificationTriageService` exposes one private loader and two public readers. `getRecentNotifications` (`lib/data/datasources/tools/chat/notification_triage_service.dart:242-262`) filters the loaded entries with `.where((e) => matchesAppFilter(e, appFilter) && !isSensitive(e))` at `:249-252`. `extractLatestOtp` (`:277-310`) calls the same loader directly at `:284` — `final entries = await _loadEntries(limit: limit);` — and never invokes `isSensitive`. Both therefore read the identical in-memory notification buffer, but only the first applies the application's sensitive-content exclusion. The `_sensitiveKeywords` list at `:87-118` includes `otp`, `one-time`, `verification code`, `password`, `passcode`, `pin`, `cvv`, `cvc`, `bank`, `transaction`, `payment`, `balance`, `account number`, and `credit card`, and `isSensitive` at `:119-122` matches them against the lowercased `title` and `body`. By construction, every notification this tool is designed to find is a notification the sibling tool refuses to return.

**The extracted secret is returned in full.** `extractOtp` (`:137-151`) applies a contextual pattern `(?:code|otp|pin|passcode|verification)[^\d]{0,24}(\d{4,8})` and falls back to any bare four-to-eight digit group, so the match is not limited to notifications that literally say "OTP". On a hit, the service returns an `OtpExtractionResult` (`:290-297`) carrying the live code plus the sending application's display name, package name, timestamp, and a 120-character body snippet. `OtpExtractionResult.toJson` (`lib/domain/tools/chat/notification_triage_service.dart:79-89`) emits `'otp': otp` unconditionally, so the secret is present in the serialized tool result. There is no redaction, masking, or truncation of the code at any point.

**No binding check ties the code to the user's own action.** `extractLatestOtp` accepts only `appFilter` and `limit` (`:277-280`); there is no transaction identifier, no correlation with a login the user initiated, and no verification that the user is the party the code is meant for. The tool returns whatever the newest matching notification contains, so an attacker-crafted notification can be used to have the agent surface the attacker's own code, and a code received on the victim's device for an attacker-initiated login can be harvested without any check that the user requested it.

**The gate is auto-executing.** The tool is registered at `lib/domain/tools/chat/tool_registry.dart:851` with `securityTier: SecurityTier.tier2Permission` at `:871` and `checkPermission: () => service.checkPermission()` at `:872`. The enforcement point at `:250-255` evaluates that permission once and never re-prompts; `checkPermission` in turn merely confirms the OS-level Notification Listener grant (`notification_triage_service.dart:196-207`), which is a single coarse toggle the user sets once. The agent loop confirms the tier semantics: `lib/presentation/screen/chat/cubit/agent_cubit.dart:759-765` pauses for human approval only when `registered.securityTier == SecurityTier.tier3Hitl`, and Tier 1 and Tier 2 fall through to `emit(ExecutingTool(...))` followed by `executeTool` at `:766`. The tier is read from a local constant fixed at registration and is never derived from model output, a gateway frame, a skill package, or a tool result, so the classification itself cannot be downgraded remotely — but the classification as written is the defect.

**Two independent off-device sinks consume the result.** In the local ReAct loop the result string is appended as `ChatMessage(role: 'tool', toolCallId: callId, name: toolName, content: resultStr)` at `agent_cubit.dart:820-825`; `_messages.map((m) => m.toWireJson())` at `:906` serializes it, and `toWireJson` (`lib/domain/entities/chat/chat_message.dart:116-127`) writes `content` verbatim into the map; the resulting `messagesToSend` is passed to `_llmRepository.streamCompletion(...)` at `:923-930`. The endpoint is the user's configured model base URL, defaulting to `https://api.openai.com/v1` at `:121` and overridden from profile settings at `:482-483` and `:491-492`. Separately, when the call originates from a gateway `tool_call_request`, `lib/domain/services/gateway/gateway_rpc_receiver.dart:148` executes the same tool and the success branch at `:166-171` returns the full parsed result map — including the `otp` field — to the remote Hermes server via `gatewayClient.sendToolCallResponse`. Both sinks are governed by the same single tier constant, which is why reclassification closes both.

**The value is also persisted.** `agent_cubit.dart:826` calls `_persistMessages()`, which writes the session history through `lib/data/datasources/local/chat/chat_local_datasource.dart:113-121` into FlutterSecureStorage — so the chat-history copy is encrypted at rest and is not itself a plaintext exposure. The stronger persistence path is the one the project's own integration test encodes: `test/integration/e2e_fase3_intelligence_test.dart:280-293` has the model follow an `extract_latest_otp` result with a `save_memory` call whose content is the extracted code. `save_memory` is Tier 1 and auto-executes (`tool_registry.dart:884`), writing into the memory vault, which is a plain SQLite database (`lib/data/datasources/local/memory/sqlite_memory_datasource.dart:16`, `databaseFileName = 'flames_memory.db'`) with no application-level encryption, so the code would be readable at rest beyond its normal validity window.

**Intent.** The repository is explicit that this is a deliberate capability — the tool description says it "Extracts the latest OTP code from captured notifications", the `notification_triage` skill is documented as reading notifications and extracting security OTP verification codes (`lib/domain/services/skills/skills_registry_service.dart:610-625`), and the deployment documentation states that Flames "requires Notification Listener permission to capture 2FA OTP codes" (`docs/connecting-to-remote-hermes.md:270`). The finding is therefore not that the feature exists, but that the control around it is inconsistent with the application's own privacy design: the product deliberately withholds these notifications from the model on one path while handing the extracted secret to the model on another, and the path that hands it over is the one that requires no per-use confirmation.

fix_pr_body:
## Problem

`extract_latest_otp` is registered at `securityTier: SecurityTier.tier2Permission`. Tier 2 tools auto-execute once Notification Listener access has been granted a single time (`tool_registry.dart:250-255`, `agent_cubit.dart:759-766`), so the tool silently extracts a live second-factor code from another app's notification and the code is then transmitted to the configured LLM endpoint and, on the gateway path, to the remote Hermes server.

This contradicts the app's own stated privacy posture: the sibling tool `read_recent_notifications` deliberately excludes exactly these notifications via `isSensitive` (`notification_triage_service.dart:87-122, 249-252`), and the project's own test is named `filters out sensitive entries for privacy` (`notification_triage_service_test.dart:375`).

## Change

Reclassify `extract_latest_otp` from Tier 2 to Tier 3 (HITL). One line in `lib/domain/tools/chat/tool_registry.dart`.

## Why this closes the boundary

All three `executeTool` call sites consult the same local `securityTier` value, so a single reclassification closes every path:

- `agent_cubit.dart:766` — reached only after the Tier 3 branch at `:760` pauses for approval.
- `agent_cubit.dart:611` — runs post-approval, already user-gated.
- `gateway_rpc_receiver.dart:148` — gated by `SecurityPolicy.requiresHitl` at `:89`; with no approval callback registered the request fails closed.

The approval sheet renders the real `request.parameters` (`action_approval_sheet.dart:45,68`), and the voice path returns `VoiceTurnNeedsApprovalFailure` rather than auto-approving (`chat_voice_prompt_dispatcher.dart:125-127`), so the gate is not bypassable from those entry points.

## Why not the alternatives

- **Applying `isSensitive` inside `extractLatestOtp`** would make every OTP notification match the keyword list and the tool would permanently return `found: false` — a feature-breaking non-fix, not a control.
- **Redacting the code from the model** is architecturally reasonable but requires redesigning how the result reaches the user (local UI surfacing), so it is out of scope for a minimal patch. Worth considering as a follow-up so the model never receives the secret at all.

## Notes

- `checkPermission` is left in place and is inert for a Tier 3 tool, since the permission branch only runs when `SecurityPolicy.requiresPermission(tier)` is true (i.e. Tier 2 only).
- Not dynamically validated: no device or emulator was available. Verification was by source trace and `dart analyze`.

title: Credentials can be transmitted over cleartext HTTP/WS because endpoint validators accept http:// and ws:// URLs
description: The app's endpoint validators accept cleartext `http://` and `ws://` URLs, and the stored credentials are then attached to whatever endpoint results: the LLM API key is sent as `Authorization: Bearer` to `$baseUrl/chat/completions` and to the TTS endpoint, and the gateway token is transmitted as the first WebSocket frame. The project's own deployment guide instructs users to configure plain-http LAN endpoints, so the credential traverses the local network unencrypted and is recoverable by anyone who can observe that segment. Critically, Android's cleartext policy does not prevent this: Flutter's HTTP/WebSocket stack is implemented in the Dart VM and never consults it, and Flutter's own equivalent gate is permissive by default on Android.
impact: A passive attacker positioned on the same network segment as the device — the home or office LAN that the project's own deployment guide targets with `http://192.168.1.100:8642/v1` — can read the bearer credential directly from the wire: the LLM API key from the `Authorization: Bearer` header of `/chat/completions` (and of the TTS request), or the Hermes gateway token from the first WebSocket frame. Either credential grants the holder the user's authority on that infrastructure: API spend and conversation access on the LLM endpoint, and device-tool invocation through the operator's gateway. Because the token is provisioned by scanning a QR code, an attacker who can present a QR code can also supply the cleartext `http://` gateway URL that produces the exposure. An on-path attacker able to modify the cleartext stream can additionally alter request and response content (integrity impact), though that requires active interception rather than passive observation. The exposure applies to every Android version the build supports, because the platform's cleartext restriction is not consulted by this application's network stack.
target: Flames Android app (ai.hermes.flames / Flutter package flutter_ai_agent) — repository /workspace/flames-audit-t196
poc_description:
1. On the target device, follow the project's documented setup (docs/connecting-to-remote-hermes.md:161 or :176) and configure a server profile with a plain-http gateway/base URL, e.g. `http://192.168.1.100:8642/v1`, supplying the Hermes `API_SERVER_KEY` as the profile token. Alternatively, scan a pairing QR whose payload contains an `http://` `gatewayUrl` — the pairing parser accepts it (pairing_parser.dart:53-55).
2. The app accepts the URL because `isAcceptableGatewayUrl` admits the `http` scheme (gateway_url.dart:15) and the settings/profile validators only require `http` or `https` (settings_cubit.dart:118-121, server_profile_cubit.dart:97-100).
3. On the same network segment, run a passive capture of the device's traffic (e.g. `tcpdump -i <iface> -A -s0 'tcp port 8642'` on the LAN, or the equivalent on the Tailscale path).

5. Observe the credential in the capture: `Authorization: Bearer <API key>` in the `/chat/completions` request (or in the `/v1/audio/speech` TTS request), or the WebSocket handshake frame `{"type":"auth","token":"<gateway token>", ...}` for the gateway connection.

remediation_steps:
1. Restrict the accepted gateway schemes to the TLS variants. `acceptedGatewayUrlSchemes` (lib/domain/services/gateway/gateway_url.dart:15) is the shared contract consulted by the profile form, the settings form and the gateway client, so narrowing it to `https` and `wss` closes those entry points in one change and `isAcceptableGatewayUrl` then rejects cleartext URLs before they can be stored.
2. Reject the `http` scheme explicitly in the pairing parser (lib/domain/tools/pairing/pairing_parser.dart:53-56) so a scanned QR code can never select a cleartext transport, and update the parser's error message so it no longer advertises HTTP as acceptable.
3. Apply the same TLS requirement to the two duplicated validators (lib/presentation/screen/settings/cubit/settings_cubit.dart:118-121, lib/presentation/screen/server_profiles/cubit/server_profile_cubit.dart:97-100) and to the settings form field validator (lib/presentation/screen/settings/settings_screen.dart:417-420), so the contract cannot drift between entry points.
4. Migrate or reject already-persisted cleartext configuration. The validators only govern new input; a device that already stored an `http://` base URL will keep using it. Reject a non-TLS base URL when settings are read from secure storage (or clear the stored value once), so the credential can never be attached to a legacy cleartext endpoint.
5. Do not rely on the Android network security policy for this issue. Declaring `android:networkSecurityConfig` with `cleartextTrafficPermitted="false"` is worthwhile defence-in-depth for any Java-side plugin traffic, but it does not govern this application's HTTP or WebSocket stack, which does not consult it. The effective control is the scheme validation in the application code. (If the platform policy is added, it must be accompanied by the code change, or the credential path remains open.)
6. Update the deployment documentation (docs/connecting-to-remote-hermes.md:161 and :176) to stop presenting `http://` endpoints as the standard option, and instead point at the TLS options already documented in the same guide (Cloudflare Tunnel, or an Nginx/Caddy TLS reverse proxy).
7. Update the test suite to assert the new contract: the cases in test/domain/services/gateway/gateway_url_test.dart that accept `http://`/`ws://` become rejection cases, and add a case asserting that a cleartext profile is refused before any socket is opened.
assumptions: Assumes the operator follows the project's own deployment guidance (plain-http LAN endpoint, docs/connecting-to-remote-hermes.md:176) or scans a pairing QR that carries an `http://` gateway URL (the pairing parser accepts `http`, pairing_parser.dart:53-55), and that a passive or on-path adversary shares that network segment — the premise of the documented LAN topology. The client-side behaviours (scheme acceptance, header attachment, auth-frame send) are static facts established from source; the platform behaviour that permits the cleartext connection is established from the engine and SDK sources at the pinned Flutter revision. Not assumed, and not demonstrated: an actual capture of the credential on a live network.
counterevidence: Actively sought constraints. (a) The strongest counterargument was that Android blocks cleartext by default, which would have limited this to API 26/27 devices — that argument is disproven, not merely unverified: the application's HTTP and WebSocket traffic does not go through the Android/OkHttp stack that enforces the policy, and Flutter's own equivalent gate is permissive on Android because the embedding never enables it. (b) On the Tailscale topology (`http://100.x.y.z:8642/v1`) the traffic is carried inside Tailscale's WireGuard tunnel and is therefore encrypted on the wire despite the `http://` scheme, so that documented configuration is materially less exposed than the LAN one; the LAN guidance (`http://192.168.1.100:8642/v1`) has no such protection. This narrows one deployment variant but does not affect the plain-LAN case. (c) The cleartext tolerance is deliberate rather than accidental: the test suite pins the accepted scheme set and exercises `http://`/`ws://` acceptance cases, so this is a product decision, which is why the remediation is framed as a policy change with an explicit migration cost. (d) A redirect to a third-party origin does not leak the credential, because `dart:io` strips sensitive headers on cross-origin redirects — checked and excluded. (e) No TLS misconfiguration was found that would also expose users on TLS endpoints: no custom HTTP client adapter, certificate callback or trust-store override exists in the application code, so the platform trust store is authoritative for `https`/`wss`. (f) Exploitation requires the attacker to already hold a network position on the segment (or to induce the user to scan an attacker-supplied QR code), and requires the user or operator to have configured a cleartext endpoint; neither is free, and both are reflected in the attack-vector and attack-complexity metrics.
confidence_rationale: Static source-only audit: no APK, emulator or device was available, so no request was ever executed against a live endpoint and this finding is explicitly **unconfirmed, not dynamically validated**. The application-layer facts are established directly from source: cleartext schemes are admitted by all four validators, and each credential-bearing client attaches the stored secret to the resulting URL. The platform-layer question that previously set the affected population has since been resolved from authoritative engine and SDK sources at the exact Flutter revision this repository pins: the connection gate is permissive by default and the Android embedding does not enable the strict mode, so `http://` and `ws://` are functional on every supported API level. What remains unexecuted is the end-to-end demonstration — a real capture showing the credential on the wire — which is why the confidence is medium rather than high.

## Summary

Credentials (the LLM API key and the Hermes gateway token) are currently attached to endpoints whose scheme only has to be one of `http`/`https`/`ws`/`wss`. This change restricts every credential-bearing endpoint to TLS (`https`/`wss`) at the points where a URL is accepted or stored.

## Rationale

- `acceptedGatewayUrlSchemes` (`lib/domain/services/gateway/gateway_url.dart:15`) is the single source of truth consulted by the profile form and the connection probe; the settings form, the settings cubit and the profile cubit each duplicate the same `http`/`https` test. Narrowing all of them to `https` closes the configuration entry points together and keeps them from drifting apart.
- The API key is sent as `Authorization: Bearer` to `$baseUrl/...` (`chat_datasource.dart:51`, `voice_output_service.dart:258`) and the gateway token is the first WebSocket frame (`gateway_client.dart:212-216`). Both are bearer credentials, so a cleartext transport is equivalent to publishing them to the network segment.
- `lib/domain/tools/pairing/pairing_parser.dart:53-56` accepts an `http://` gateway URL from a scanned QR code, which is attacker-controllable input; it must not be able to select a cleartext transport.
- The platform does not compensate: this application's HTTP and WebSocket traffic is served by the Dart runtime, which does not consult Android's cleartext policy, and Flutter's own equivalent gate is permissive on Android because the embedding never enables strict mode. A `network-security-config` entry would therefore not close this path — the scheme validation in the application code is the effective control.

## Impact and migration

Endpoints that are plain HTTP today — the documented LAN setup in particular (`docs/connecting-to-remote-hermes.md:176`) — will be rejected with the existing validation message. Operators must expose those gateways over TLS (the same guide already documents Cloudflare Tunnel and an Nginx/Caddy TLS reverse proxy). This trade-off is intentional: bearer credentials should not be provisioned over cleartext. A follow-up is needed for values already persisted by an earlier version, since these validators only govern new input.

## Testing

- `test/domain/services/gateway/gateway_url_test.dart` must be updated: its cases asserting that `http://`/`ws://` are accepted become the negative cases.
- `test/data/datasources/remote/gateway/gateway_client_test.dart` should add a case asserting a `ws://` profile is refused before any socket is opened.
- Run the suite for the touched packages.

title: Notification text from any installed app reaches the agent prompt with no data/instruction separation and can drive auto-executing Tier-1 device tools
description: Flames reads the notification title and body of every app on the device through its notification-listener service and returns them to the language model as a tool result (read_recent_notifications, extract_latest_otp). Those strings are authored by whichever app posted the notification, not by Flames and not by the user, yet nothing on the path marks them as untrusted, delimits them, caps their length, or scans them. The app already ships a prompt-injection scanner but applies it only to imported skill text. The same model can then call tools that execute with no user confirmation, including clipboard_write, send_local_notification, save_memory and speak_text, and, because read_web_page is declared permissioned but registered without a permission checker, read_web_page, which can carry on-device data off the device in a URL. Unconfirmed, not dynamically validated — this is a source-only audit with no emulator, no device and no running app, so no payload was executed and no tool call was induced.
impact: A malicious or merely compromised app installed on the same device can post a notification whose title/body contains instructions, and those instructions enter the agent's context with the same standing as the user's own request. Because the reachable tools need no approval, the injected text can cause the device to copy attacker-chosen content to the clipboard (clipboard_write), display a forged notification (send_local_notification), speak text aloud (speak_text), write an entry into the memory vault (save_memory) — which is later re-injected as a role:"system" message on any turn whose prompt matches — or register a geofence (register_geofence). Combined with clipboard_read (Tier 1) and read_web_page (declared Tier 2 but registered without a permission checker, so it auto-executes), on-device content can be staged and then transmitted to an attacker-controlled URL in a query string, with no permission prompt and no human-in-the-loop step. The concrete end-to-end result is model- and payload-dependent and was not demonstrated. Tier-3 actions (make_phone_call, open_whatsapp_chat, calendar_create_event, schedule_reminder) remain behind the approval modal and were not bypassed.

technical_analysis:
**Relationship to the accessibility-channel finding.** The scan already carries a report for the same class of defect — untrusted text reaching the prompt as an unframed tool result — evidenced on the accessibility channel (ui_find_elements), fixed in lib/data/datasources/tools/chat/accessibility_inspector_service.dart. This report covers a different channel: a different data source, a different Android permission, and a different runtime trigger. The accessibility report's remediation text explicitly leaves notification text, web-page text and recalled memory unframed. The generic point (tool results are unframed) is shared; the notification-specific evidence, permission and trigger are not.

**1. Collection — attacker-authored strings, no cap.** FlamesNotificationListenerService.processNotification copies Notification.EXTRA_TITLE / EXTRA_TEXT / EXTRA_BIG_TEXT / EXTRA_SUB_TEXT verbatim into an in-memory buffer. Only the number of entries is capped (MAX_BUFFER_SIZE = 100); the strings themselves have no length limit. packageName is whatever app posted the notification.
